{"stdout":"# Editorial playbook — AI Edge Briefing

You are producing today's edition of a daily briefing on frontier AI. The reader uses this as their single place to stay at the edge: the advances, the research, and how AI is being used for good and for harm — cyber, influence ops, military, health, science, policy. It is not a "fun uses of AI" newsletter. It is raw, factual, sourced.

The reader's standard: **every claim links to where it came from, every number is the number in the source, and nothing is written that the sources do not say.** If you cannot source it, it does not go in.

## 0. Setup

1. Work in the repo root. Determine today's date in **America/Toronto**: `TZ=America/Toronto date +%F`. That is the edition date, `DATE`.
2. `ls data/` — the previous edition tells you the cutoff. The coverage window (`WINDOW`) is from the previous edition's `generated_at` to now (if there is no previous edition, the 24 hours before now). Write it down as absolute timestamps in both UTC and ET; you will hand it to the subagents. Read the previous edition so you do not repeat it; a story already covered goes in again **only if there is a new development**, flagged `update`, and the bullets report only the new facts.
3. `node scripts/build.js --topics` — the existing topic slugs. Reuse them; only coin a new slug when nothing fits.
   `node scripts/build.js --storylines` — the open storylines (id, status, name, frame). An item that is a development in one of those arcs is **filed under it** (see §3, `storylines`). The daily never creates a storyline; the Monday Week in Review does.
4. Every day is a daily edition, Mondays included. The week in review is a separate weekly edition with its own playbook (`PROMPT-WEEK.md`) and its own routine — never part of the daily file.

## 0b. Keep your own context small — it is most of what this edition costs

Every turn you take re-sends this whole conversation. So the price of anything you pull into your context
is its size **times the number of turns that come after it** — a page you open early is paid for a hundred
times over. Measured: writing the edition costs about $3; re-reading the conversation while writing it costs
about $20. None of the rules below cost you a source, a check or an item. They stop you paying rent on text
you have already used.

1. **Write files with `Write`, and change them with `Edit`.** Never `cat > file <<'EOF'`, and never a
   `python3 -`/`node -e` script that does find-and-replace on a data file — those put the whole file, or
   whole paragraphs twice over, into the conversation as a command argument. `Edit` sends only the line that
   changes.
2. **Never print a file back out after writing it.** You know what you wrote. To check it, run the
   validator — it prints errors, not contents.
3. **Read the part you need.** `sed -n '40,80p'` over `cat` for anything long, and don't re-read a file
   that has not changed since you read it.
4. **`node scripts/fetch.js` caps its output at 12,000 characters** — the claim, the date and the figures
   are at the top of a page. Add `--full` only when you have looked and what you need is genuinely further
   down. Don't pipe it through `head` as well; the cap is already there.
5. **Let the subagents hold the raw material.** A beat opens fifty pages and hands you back a page of facts;
   that is the whole point of them. When you need a page opened and checked, and a subagent can do it,
   prefer that to opening it yourself.
6. Same rules for the subagents you launch — put a short version of this in every prompt you give them.

None of this licenses checking less. If a fact needs a source opened, open it. Verify everything §2 says to
verify. This is about what you keep afterwards, not what you look at.

## 1. Sweep the sources — four beats in parallel

Read `SOURCES.md`. Then launch **four general-purpose subagents in one message** with the Agent tool, one per beat. Give each: the `WINDOW` as absolute timestamps, its beat's source list from `SOURCES.md`, the **Sourcing rules** below verbatim, and the return format. Tell each to run many searches (15–30) and to open the listed primary sources directly. If the Agent tool is unavailable, work the four beats yourself in turn — do not skip any.

- **Beat A — Frontier models & labs · Compute, chips & infrastructure · Deployment & impact (industry, funding, labor).** SOURCES.md §1, §7, §8.
- **Beat B — Research & papers (incl. safety, alignment, evals).** SOURCES.md §2. arXiv new listings (cs.AI, cs.LG, cs.CL, cs.CR, cs.CV, cs.RO), Hugging Face papers, alphaXiv, Nature/Science, lab research blogs, Epoch, METR, AISI, CAISI, Apollo, Redwood, Alignment Forum. Prefer papers with a notable quantitative result, from major labs/universities, or drawing significant attention. Return arXiv IDs and author institutions.
- **Beat C — Security, misuse & threat intelligence · Military, defense & geopolitics.** SOURCES.md §3, §4. AI-enabled intrusions and malware, fraud and scams, deepfakes, influence operations, surveillance, prompt injection and agent exploits, model theft / illicit distillation, bio/chem misuse reports; procurement, deployment, autonomous weapons, export controls, national strategies.
- **Beat D — Health, science & medicine · Policy, regulation & law.** SOURCES.md §5, §6. Clinical results, FDA/Health Canada/WHO actions, drug discovery, AI for science, biosecurity; legislation, regulation, enforcement, court rulings and filings, government reports, standards — US federal and state, EU, UK, Canada, China, international bodies.

**Subagent return format** — one block per item, then a short list of rejected candidates and why:

```
SECTION: <one of the eight section names>
HEADLINE: <factual, specific, max 18 words, no hype>
PUBLISHED: <date/time and timezone exactly as the source shows it>
SOURCES: one per line — <publisher> | <exact URL> | primary or report   (only URLs actually opened or seen in search results; never constructed)
FACTS: 2–5 bullets, each a verifiable fact from a linked source, numbers/units/baselines exactly as written, naming which source
FLAGS: company-claim | single-source | preprint | update  (any that apply)
```

**Sourcing rules (give to subagents verbatim):**
1. Only include facts that appear in a source you opened (WebFetch) or in the text of a search result. No inference, speculation, predictions or "this could mean". No hype adjectives.
2. Every item links to the specific article, paper or document — never a homepage or index page. Link the primary source whenever one exists (paper, company post, government document, filing, court record) plus independent reporting. Aim for 2+ sources on significant items; if only one outlet has it, flag `single-source`.
3. Confirm the publication date is inside the window. If the date cannot be determined, drop the item. Older stories qualify only if something new happened inside the window, and only the new facts are reported (flag `update`).
4. Attribute claims: "OpenAI says…", "according to The Record…". Company-reported benchmarks, user counts, revenue and capability claims get `company-claim` unless independently verified. Research that is not peer reviewed gets `preprint`.
5. Quote numbers exactly as the source writes them, with units and the comparison baseline. Do not round, convert or compute new figures.
6. If `WebFetch` refuses a page, fetch it directly with `node scripts/fetch.js <url>` — the sites we read have given permission for direct reads, and the fetcher identifies itself. Use only what the returned text actually says; if it comes back as a paywall stub, a login page or nothing usable, fall back to search-result text or another source and say in the bullet where the figures came from. Never use archive or cache sites, and never cite a URL whose content you did not see. Sites that refuse `WebFetch` are listed in SOURCES.md.
7. Skip consumer tips, "fun uses", prompt guides, listicles, opinion pieces without new facts, minor feature updates, unsourced rumours, and small funding rounds unless strategically notable (US$100M+, or a frontier lab / defense / health / security company).
8. When in doubt, leave it out.

After the beats return, run a few **gap-check searches** yourself for anything a beat may have missed (WebSearch: "AI" + Pentagon / drone; "AI" + FDA / hospital; "AI" + scam / deepfake / influence operation; "AI" + export controls / data center power; "AI" + lawsuit / ruling; plus Techmeme and Hacker News front page), restricted to the window.

## 2. Verify and select

Merge the beats' returns. De-duplicate across beats and against previous editions. Then, for each candidate:
- Open the primary source. Confirm the headline and every number/date/name you intend to use. A secondary report of a paper links the paper. A report of a court ruling links the ruling or docket where possible.
- Prefer two independent sources for anything contested, surprising, or about a specific actor (a named threat group, a company's claim about a rival, a casualty figure).
- Drop: opinion pieces without new facts, product marketing with no numbers, speculation, "could" / "may" stories, anything you cannot open, anything older than the window without a new development.
- Spot-verify: open (WebFetch, or `node scripts/fetch.js` if it refuses) the key source for every item you will mention in the summary and for every figure in the summary; confirm date, numbers and URL yourself. Remove anything you cannot confirm.
- Keep: model/system releases with benchmarks or capabilities; papers with a result (state the result); documented misuse and threat-intel reports (name actors, counts, dates); military and government procurement/deployment; clinical and scientific results; regulation, enforcement, court decisions; compute/chip/energy facts with figures; large-scale deployments and measured impacts, good or bad.

## 3. Write the edition — `data/DATE.json`

Schema (see `data/2026-09-11.json` for a full example once it exists):

```json
{
  "date": "YYYY-MM-DD",
  "edition": "daily",
  "generated_at": "<ISO-8601 UTC timestamp>",
  "window": "e.g. 10 Sep 11:00 → 11 Sep 11:00 UTC",
  "title": "The episode's name — 3 to 10 words, a statement: who did what, or what changed. No period, no colon, no figure that is not in the summary. It is read in podcast apps as 'Name [2 Oct 2026]', so it must stand alone.",
  "summary": ["paragraph 1", "paragraph 2"],
  "sections": [
    {
      "name": "<one of the eight section names below>",
      "items": [
        {
          "headline": "Specific, factual, one line — who did what, with the key number",
          "sources": [{ "name": "Anthropic", "url": "https://..." }, { "name": "Reuters", "url": "https://..." }],
          "bullets": ["What was announced/found, with numbers.", "Why it matters / what it changes.", "Caveats, what is unverified, what to watch."],
          "topics": ["anthropic", "threat-intel", "cyber-offense"],
          "storylines": ["ai-enabled-hacking"],
          "impact": "beneficial" | "harmful" | "mixed" | "neutral",
          "flags": ["company-claim" | "single-source" | "preprint" | "update"]
        }
      ]
    }
  ]
}
```

**Section names** (exactly these; omit a section if it has nothing that day):
1. `Frontier models & labs` — releases, capabilities, benchmarks, lab announcements, safety cases, system cards.
2. `Research & papers` — papers with results: new methods, evals, interpretability, alignment, scaling. State the result and the number.
3. `Security, misuse & threat intelligence` — threat-intel reports, documented attacks using AI, influence operations, scams/deepfakes, model vulnerabilities, prompt injection, jailbreaks, agent security.
4. `Military, defense & geopolitics` — procurement, deployment, autonomous weapons, export controls, national strategies, China/US/EU competition.
5. `Health, science & medicine` — clinical results, FDA actions, drug discovery, AI-for-science results, hospital deployments and their measured outcomes.
6. `Policy, regulation & law` — legislation, regulation, enforcement, court rulings, government reports, standards.
7. `Compute, chips & infrastructure` — chips, fabs, datacenters, power, capex figures, funding rounds and deals with numbers.
8. `Deployment & impact` — large-scale rollouts, labor effects, measured societal effects, incidents, the good and the bad in practice.

**Summary**: 2–3 paragraphs, ~150–250 words. The three to five things that matter most today, stated as facts, with the numbers. No throat-clearing, no "in today's edition".

**Headlines**: one line, specific, factual. "Anthropic report: Russian state group GTG-20006 used Claude to automate espionage against Ukrainian and European governments" — not "Anthropic releases threat report".

**Bullets**: 2–4 per item. First bullet is the fact with the number. Then significance. Then caveats — say plainly what is unverified, what the source did not say, what to watch. Write in complete sentences. Never pad.

**Sources**: 1–4 per item, primary first. `name` is the publisher (Anthropic, arXiv, Reuters, FDA, Court docket), not the article title.

**Topics**: 1–4 lowercase-hyphen slugs per item. Reuse existing slugs (`node scripts/build.js --topics`). Canonical slugs to prefer: `anthropic`, `openai`, `google-deepmind`, `meta`, `xai`, `mistral`, `deepseek`, `qwen`, `nvidia`, `microsoft`, `amazon`, `apple`, `threat-intel`, `cyber-offense`, `cyber-defense`, `influence-ops`, `scams-fraud`, `deepfakes`, `prompt-injection`, `agents`, `agent-security`, `alignment`, `interpretability`, `evals`, `open-weights`, `reasoning-models`, `scaling`, `compute`, `chips`, `export-controls`, `energy`, `datacenters`, `china`, `eu-ai-act`, `us-federal-policy`, `us-state-policy`, `uk`, `copyright`, `privacy`, `military`, `autonomous-weapons`, `pentagon`, `healthcare`, `fda`, `drug-discovery`, `bio-risk`, `ai-for-science`, `robotics`, `labor`, `education`, `elections`, `surveillance`, `child-safety`, `incidents`, `funding`, `earnings`. Add an entity slug (company, agency, named group) when the story is about that entity.

**Storylines** (optional; usually one, at most two): the ids from `node scripts/build.js --storylines` whose arc this item advances — a new development in *that story*, not merely the same topic. Only existing ids with status `live` or `proposed`; the validator rejects unknown or resolved ids. Omit the key when the item belongs to none. Never coin an id here.

**Impact** (optional but encouraged): `beneficial`, `harmful`, `mixed`, or `neutral` — the demonstrated effect in the story, not your prediction.

**Flags** (include every one that applies; omit the key if none): `company-claim` — a company-reported benchmark, user count, revenue or capability claim not independently verified; `single-source` — only one outlet has it; `preprint` — research not peer reviewed; `update` — a story covered in an earlier edition, with new facts only.

**Style**: plain, declarative, numbers over adjectives. Attribute claims ("Anthropic says", "the paper reports", "according to the filing"). No hype, no hedging language beyond what the sources support. British or American spelling — either, consistently.

**Absolute rules**:
- Never invent a URL, a number, a quote, a name, or a date. If unsure, open the source again.
- Never write a bullet you could not point to a sentence in the source for.
- Never link a URL you did not open in this session.
- Quote numbers exactly as the source writes them, with units and baseline. Never round, convert, or compute new figures.
- Link the specific article, paper or document — never a homepage or index page (the validator rejects these).

# Sources

The sweep list for every edition. **Primary** sources (labs, papers, governments, court filings, security vendors' own reports) are always preferred for the link beside a headline; **secondary** sources (press, newsletters, aggregators) are used to discover stories and as corroboration. Who May Overrule the Agent? Evidence-Gated Authority in LLM Review Institutions
https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.05390
arXiv:2611.05390v1 Announce Type: new
Abstract: Multi-agent language-model systems often add a reviewer to improve an upstream agent's decision. Yet a reviewer can both repair errors and replace decisions that were already correct. We study this as a problem of institutional jurisdiction: conditional on the same proposal, task information, model, and review output, when is the reviewer authorized to make its recommendation binding? We compare broad override authority with an evidence gate that permits replacement only after the reviewer produces a mechanically valid record of a binding-constraint violation and a compliant repair. Across two locally run open-weight models, 96 spatial-policy tasks, and a 96-task portfolio-transfer benchmark, the gate sharply reduces corruption of correct proposals while retaining most repairs of violations. The directions of this tradeoff are partly implied by the rule; its magnitude depends on reviewer transitions and upstream proposal states. A prospective validation then gives the reviewer an explicit choice to retain, replace, or escalate. This eliminates correct-proposal corruption for Qwen, but Mistral still replaces all 48 correct proposals; Qwen also declines every welfare-only repair that Mistral frequently attempts. Thus interface design changes reviewer behavior but is not a model-independent safeguard. The result is not that restricted review is universally better. It is that reviewer competence, action interface, and binding jurisdiction jointly determine both the correction domain and the corruption surface.

Agent Harness Awareness: Turning Verified Telemetry into Operational Control for Tool-Using Agents
https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.05391
arXiv:2611.05391v1 Announce Type: new
Abstract: Tool descriptions tell an agent what an action can do, but they do not necessarily reveal whether that action is healthy or suitable at the moment of use. Execution harnesses often possess this information through monitors, traces, and recent failures while the model choosing the next action does not. We call this gap operational blindness. We introduce Agent Harness Awareness, a trust-separated design in which the host supplies a small, fresh, verified state snapshot before a consequential action while retaining measurement, enforcement, evaluation, and final dispatch authority. We test its tools-and-network instance with ToolRoute, a controlled isolation benchmark that holds the task and candidate semantics constant and varies the operational information available to the model. In a 216-decision ablation across GPT-5.6 Sol, Claude Sonnet 5, and Gemini 3.7 Flash, verified tool-health state reduced mean observable policy regret by 96.9% against a same-shape neutral control (4,252 ms to 131 ms) and raised single-dispatch completion from 69.4% to 95.8%. In a separate 27-decision end-to-end replication with live local TCP/HTTP execution, OpenTelemetry client spans, and Toxiproxy-injected faults, verified state reduced mean regret from 8,956 ms to 0 ms (zero excess observable operational cost) and completed the live action in 9/9 model-by-fault cases versus 5/9 for the neutral control. These studies establish the tools-and-network instance of Agent Harness Awareness: selected host telemetry materially improves pre-dispatch operational choice. Runtime state, hardware pressure, economics, retry-aware recovery, and heterogeneous selection remain open empirical extensions of the same architecture.

Chainalysis warns all users hit in cyber breach involving ‘agentic’ techniques | The Record from Recorded Future News
Chainalysis disclosed the breach on Wednesday night

# Chainalysis warns all users hit in cyber breach involving ‘agentic’ techniques
Chainalysis, the blockchain analytics company, said Wednesday night that some information belonging to all its users — which its website says include those in the law enforcement and national security sectors — had been exposed in a cyberattack.
The company initially disclosed a breach on Oct. 30, although at the time said it had found no evidence that authentication credentials or session tokens had been accessed.
In its latest update , posted Wednesday night, the company said it had discovered “certain customer information including names, usernames, password hashes and live tokens for all Chainalysis users were exposed to a malicious actor.”
The perpetrator was not identified. Chainalysis previously said it had “detected an external actor using offensive agentic techniques to gain unauthorized access to Chainalysis systems and internal tools.” It has not explained what it meant by “offensive agentic techniques.”
The company initially told customers the breach came amid what it described as “an industry-wide rise in AI-driven cyberattacks.” Although it initially mentioned agentic techniques, it did not explicitly say its own breach was caused by an AI agent.
Chainalysis said it had engaged “world-class third-party cybersecurity experts” to help investigate the incident and strengthen its defenses.
Its statement did not specify whether every category of information was exposed for every user, nor did it say how many users it has.
According to its website, Chainalysis says it provides services to more than 1,500 customers across sectors including law enforcement, cryptocurrency and regular finance, regulators and national security.
“At this time we continue to have no evidence that any investigations data has been accessed or Chainalysis attribution data has been manipulated,” the company said Wednesday night.
All users will have to reset their passwords and rotate API keys as appropriate, the company said, also urging affected customers to visit its login page directly rather than follow links in password-reset emails.
Chainalysis did not explain what it meant by “live tokens” nor say how the exposed passwords had been hashed. Certain password hashes can be cracked to recover the original password, while active authentication tokens may allow attackers to access accounts without passwords.
The company also said Wednesday night that some customers' accounts on its Know Your Transaction service (KYT) — used to monitor cryptocurrency transactions for suspicious activity — appeared to have been accessed.
The suspected account access was disclosed amid widening disruption to the company’s services as Chainalysis provided updates on its ongoing investigation.
The company said some customers’ passwords had been exposed in an “on-path attack,” in which an attacker intercepts communications between users and a service.
An email to affected customers described an “ongoing multifront cyberattack” but did not identify the other fronts. It said the interception method had been contained and remediated, affected accounts were being locked and there was no evidence they had been accessed improperly.
Forty minutes later, Chainalysis said “abnormal activity” had prompted it to take KYT's user interface and API, other address-screening products and its login page offline.
Customers who had just been instructed to reset their passwords were told doing so was not immediately possible.
The shutdown expanded restrictions imposed Monday, when the company took its Reactor investigations tool and Data Solutions product offline as a precaution but kept its compliance transaction-monitoring products running. Chainalysis describes those products as important to detecting money laundering across the cryptocurrency ecosystem.
The company said it planned to begin restoring KYT and Address Screening on Thursday, after customers submitted trusted IP addresses to be added to an allowlist. Customers would then be able to reset passwords and rotate API keys.
It gave no date for restoring Reactor, Data Solutions or another product, Chain (Beta), and did not explain how customers were screening transactions while KYT was offline.
Chainalysis has also not said whether the password interception, exposure of hashes and tokens, and suspected unauthorized account access involved the same attacker or methods.
A spokesperson said they were unable to share more information than was provided in the blog.

# French bank confirms cyber heist, hackers suspected to have stolen an estimated $133 million
A major French banking firm confirmed it experienced a “sophisticated attack” following reports that hackers stole an estimated $133 million from the firm.
Crédit Mutuel Arkéa said in a press notice that the attackers were able to make transfers using the bank’s own account after compromising an unnamed supplier. The statement stressed customer accounts were not accessed and that the incident would not impact customers’ assets.
Details about the incident were first reported on Monday by ZachXBT, a pseudonymous American blockchain investigator who subsequently named Arkéa as the alleged victim and said the attack had run over several days. ZachXBT estimated the size of the theft at more than $133 million, based on withdrawals from cryptocurrency exchange accounts and transactions intending to launder the assets.
In its statement Wednesday evening, Arkéa declined to confirm the estimated loss figure but said it could “validate the order of magnitude.” It said: “As soon as the attack was detected, the necessary measures were taken under existing crisis procedures. The incident is now under control.”
The bank disputed local reports in French media alleging the attackers had gained access through Fortuneo, its online banking subsidiary, and used it to make the initial transfers.

GRAPEVINE, Texas — Data scientists and other technical specialists were embedded next to uniformed military personnel inside U.S. Transportation Command’s global operations center for the first time during Operation Epic Fury to rapidly prototype AI-enabled tools in support of real-world warfare needs.

Those experts generated roughly “33 apps in just the first two weeks alone of OEF,” Transcom’s Chief Data and AI Officer Ryan Samuelson told DefenseScoop.

In an exclusive interview at the National Defense Transportation Association’s annual Fall meeting in Texas last week, Samuelson shed new light on Transcom’s use of AI and the Maven Smart System to accelerate strategic decision-making and data-sharing over the course of the Iran war.

“Decision advantage is how you shape outcomes ahead of when you need to actually move,” he said.

# ‘The power of it’

Transcom is responsible for moving troops and cargo worldwide for all U.S. combatant commands and defense agencies, and also transferring sick and injured troops to medical facilities for specialized treatments and recovery.

The Joint Distribution Process Analysis Center — or JDPAC — operates as the command’s analytic, engineering, and modeling engine within the global defense transportation network.

Transcom is known as an influential early adopter of Palantir’s Maven Smart System in the U.S. military enterprise. That operational AI and data-fusion software platform grew out of the Defense Department’s Project Maven, which launched nearly a decade ago.

MSS pulls disparate real-time data streams — such as satellite imagery, sensor telemetry, radar, flight paths, ship trackers and classified intelligence — into a single interface and uses computer vision and automated detection models to identify, track, and categorize potential military targets and other assets of interest.

It’s built on Palantir’s Ontology, which the company describes as “an operational layer” that “sits on top of the digital assets integrated into” the platform (like datasets and models) and connects them to their real-world counterparts (like facilities and equipment).

“I don’t want to be particular to a certain vendor — but I will tell you, in the Maven Smart System Palantir Ontology — the reason JDPAC actually was the first in Transcom to use it was the power of it. What we realized is there’s not much else, at least right now, on the market that has the ontology to be able to put in the data, to be able to put in the apps, to have the secure development. It is the most powerful tool,” Samuelson said. “The ability to operate within that, to be able to share, is really, really powerful.”

According to the CDAO , when President Donald Trump initiated Operation Epic Fury in February, Transcom’s leaders instructed data scientists and engineers from JDPAC to work side-by-side with the command’s operators.

“So, instead of those folks being in a different building and having their own work processes that would get an email or something, we put them on the floor so that they could see on all the screens the maneuver elements, the force flow, and what was happening in real time with Iranian counterattacks and U.S. attacks,” Samuelson told DefenseScoop.

Transcom’s operational staff were directed to bring problems to the data and tech experts, who would then build prototypes to help solve them in real time as the conflict unfolded.

Samuelson said he tasked his team to deliver a minimum viable product within 24 hours, gather feedback, and continuously iterate to refine their tools. Everything was connected and deployed in MSS, and the team generated dozens of digital apps and dashboards.

Some of those prototypes are still in use today.

“What did that allow us to do? I’ll give you examples. And it goes all the way from our political advisor to units at echelon that could actually use the tools,” including other combatant commands, Samuelson said.

# ‘Work at the speed of war’

From the start of Epic Fury, Transcom’s political advisor had to make sense of what Samuelson said were “all these State Department cables that were flowing in.”

The tech embeds on the operations floor quickly built an AI tool that could scrape all of those cables and summarize the ones that would likely impact Transcom’s mission set, such as those related to contested logistics or access basing and overflight restrictions.

Instead of humans having to sift through hundreds of pages of material to do that as they were coming in, the bot was actively looking and generating its own reports and query responses.

“We ended up taking the tool and all of the data that we dumped in Maven Smart System — when planes are moving, what the cargo flows were, all of that — and over a 24-hour period, our bot would look at all of that. And then [Transcom Commander Gen. Randall Reed] could come in every morning and go, ‘What happened in the last 24 hours?’ And in a matter of about 15 seconds, it would spit out a summary of, ‘This is your movements. Here’s how many were late, et cetera, et cetera,’” Samuelson said. “That used to take a team of probably four to five people hours to kind of curate that and give that [analysis].”

When asked what commercial frontier AI models supported the work, he told DefenseScoop that the team used Palantir’s AI Hivemind product in MSS, which orchestrates, trains and re-trains AI agents.

“We could easily say, ‘Hey, I now want you to take on this persona,’ or ‘I now want you to also add this,’” Samuelson said.

Separately, the embeds also created tools that fused data and analytics on munitions use to help the operators anticipate potential demand and start positioning supplies before the formal requests arrived.

Samuelson said many of the details about other bots and apps that were generated in the operation are classified. He mentioned tools built to address gaps in the Transcom fuel team’s data and analysis capabilities, as well as data streams from aircraft and watercraft downrange about health and maintenance that were changing rapidly in real time.

Because Transcom leads a complex, global logistics network to move, equip and support the joint force, officials knew that when major military operations launch, the command would receive heaps of requests from DOD components about how combat power would be aggregated.

“What we did for OEF — and really had started prior to that — is, ‘I don’t get phone calls, and I’m not going to reply with PowerPoint and emails. I’m going to send you a link that has all of that information.’ So, for [U.S. Central Command], on the Centcom commander’s dashboard, are actual datafeeds that were created at Transcom that are still on our dashboards — but we just open up a link and now they can see the exact same stuff. They don’t have to recreate it. We don’t have to push them information,” Samuelson explained. “It’s live data that’s available to both the Transcom commander and any supported combatant command.”

He said “about half” of the 33 bots and tools Transcom prototyped early into the operation are still “in production” and being used by military personnel today.

“If we want to work at the speed of war, then we need to be able to see that constantly and fine tune our processes and day to day, so we can rapidly scale to war and we are better integrated,” the Transcom CDAO told DefenseScoop.

Key Points

- OpenAI published a policy blueprint and a series of commitments that it pledged to apply to company-owned and -operated data centers in the future.

- The company said it will solicit community input around the projects, publish construction plans and protect ratepayers.

- Voters issued a stinging rebuke of data centers in the midterms after opposition to the facilities mounted over the summer.

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman speaking at Oracle AI World in Las Vegas on Oct. 27, 2026.
CNBC

OpenAI reaffirmed its promise to pay the full cost of powering data centers as part of a series of commitments the company published Thursday, two days after voters at the polls roundly rejected the rapid expansion of AI.
The artificial intelligence company said in its commitments that for data centers it owns and operates, it will solicit community input, publish construction plans and stay away from use of non-disclosure agreements with public officials. Additionally, in a policy blueprint, OpenAI encouraged policymakers to enact similar commitments as laws.

"What we're doing with this blueprint is really laying out the best lessons that we have learned and committing to applying them as they go forward," OpenAI Chief Global Affairs Officer Chris Lehane told reporters during a Wednesday briefing. "This will help ensure that there is a very high floor in terms of how people move forward."
On Tuesday, Americans issued a stinging rebuke of data centers at the polls. Out of 41 local ballot measures across 10 states, voters backed restrictions or rejected pro-development measures for all but one, according to an analysis by Ballotpedia and additional results gathered by CNBC on Wednesday.
Opposition to AI data centers mounted swiftly over the summer across both sides of the political aisle. Consumers grappling with inflation, rising grocery prices and stubbornly high prices at the pump grew worried that the facilities could exacerbate environmental harms, raise utility bills and contribute to job loss. For many, they became a physical manifestation of the widespread antipathy and anxiety around AI.
AI companies like OpenAI depend on AI data centers to serve customers and develop new models, and they're seeking to build out as rapidly as possible to meet demand. In February, OpenAI told investors that it's targeting $600 billion in total compute spend by 2030, and the company has since announced massive data center projects in Georgia and Ohio .
OpenAI has repeatedly pledged to protect ratepayers and invest in local communities this year, and Lehane said the company's latest commitments build on many of its previous initiatives. He said the policy blueprint has been in the works since August, and that he met with dozens of lawmakers and candidates since then.

"Having these conversations now actually helps put more energy into the momentum, so that when people come back in late January, new Congress is in in session, a lot of the work is being done in advance," Lehane said.

results:
The search turned up two sets of OpenAI commitments, but nothing dated November 2026 specifically.

**Stargate Community plans (January 2026):** OpenAI announced a locally tailored plan for each Stargate site, shaped by resident and regulator input. The company says it will fund new generation, transmission, and grid upgrades so its operations don't raise local electricity costs. The company promises to fund new power generation, transmission upgrades, and grid infrastructure required by its operations without passing costs to existing ratepayers. It also pledged to minimize water use. Critics are skeptical: one report notes that critics caution that funding alone may be insufficient, as environmental groups and local critics highlight water use, emissions, and scrubbed data-centre projects.

**Effingham County, Georgia (July 2026):** This is the most concrete example. OpenAI's Project Camellia commitments include $80 million in community benefits over the life of the project, informed by the community and directed toward local priorities such as schools, public safety, health care, utilities, workforce training, housing. To hold the company to these, an annual publicly available audit by an independent firm will be conducted and released. On ratepayers, under Georgia Public Service Commission rules, those costs cannot be passed on to existing ratepayers. Community input is being gathered at a public open house on July 23, and that feedback will help shape a Georgia Community Compact. The Compact is meant to translate community priorities into specific commitments and clear accountability measures as the project develops.

**Gaps:** I found no results from November 2026, so any policy blueprint or update from that month is not covered here. The Georgia Community Compact's status is also unclear from these results. A follow-up search for "Georgia Community Compact" or OpenAI's newest data center policy posts would be the next step.

DEPARTMENT OF HEALTH AND HUMAN SERVICES

Food and Drug Administration

21 CFR Part 864

[Docket No. FDA-2026-N-12384]


Medical Devices; Hematology and Pathology Devices; Classification 
of the Digital Cervical Cytology Slide Imaging System With Artificial 
Intelligence Algorithm

AGENCY: Food and Drug Administration, HHS.

ACTION: Final amendment; final order.

-----------------------------------------------------------------------

SUMMARY: The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) is classifying the 
digital cervical cytology slide imaging system with artificial 
intelligence algorithm into class II (special controls). The special 
controls that apply to the device type are identified in this order and 
will be part of the codified language for classification of the digital 
cervical cytology slide imaging system with artificial intelligence 
algorithm. We are taking this action because we have determined that 
classifying the device into class II will provide a reasonable 
assurance of the safety and effectiveness of the device. We believe 
this action will also enhance patients' access to beneficial innovative 
devices, in part by reducing regulatory burdens.

DATES: This order is effective November 5, 2026. The classification was 
applicable on January 31, 2024.

FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT: Arpita Roy, Center for Devices and 
Radiological Health, Food and Drug Administration, 10903 New Hampshire 
Ave., Bldg. 66, Rm. 3302, Silver Spring, MD 20993-0002, 240-402-4807, 
[email protected].

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:

I. Background

    Upon request, FDA (the Agency or we) has classified the digital 
cervical cytology slide imaging system with artificial intelligence 
algorithm into class II (special controls), which we have determined 
will provide a reasonable assurance of the safety and effectiveness of 
the device. In addition, we believe this action will enhance patients' 
access to beneficial innovation, in part by reducing regulatory burdens 
by placing the device into a lower device class than the automatic 
class III assignment.
    The automatic assignment of class III occurs by operation of law 
and without any action by FDA, regardless of the level of risk posed by 
the new device. Any device that was not in commercial distribution 
before May 28, 1976, is automatically classified into, and remains 
within, class III and requires premarket approval unless and until FDA 
takes an action to classify or reclassify the device (21 U.S.C. 
360c(f)(1)). We refer to these devices as ``postamendments devices'' 
because they were not in commercial distribution prior to the date of 
enactment of the Medical Device Amendments of 1976, which amended the 
Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (FD&C Act).
    FDA may take a variety of actions in appropriate circumstances to 
classify or reclassify a device into class I or II. We may issue an 
order finding a new device to be substantially equivalent under section 
513(i) of the FD&C Act (21 U.S.C. 360c(i)) to a predicate device that 
does not require premarket approval. We determine whether a new device 
is substantially equivalent to a predicate device by means of the 
procedures for premarket notification under section 510(k) of the FD&C 
Act (21 U.S.C. 360(k)) and part 807 (21 CFR part 807).
    FDA may also classify a device through ``De Novo'' classification, 
a common name for the process authorized under section 513(f)(2) of the 
FD&C Act (see also part 860, subpart D (21 CFR part 860, subpart D)). 
Section 207 of the Food and Drug Administration Modernization Act of 
1997 (Pub. L. 105-115) established the first procedure for De Novo 
classification. Section 607 of the Food and Drug Administration Safety 
and Innovation Act (Pub. L. 112-144) modified the De Novo 
classification process by adding a second procedure. A device sponsor 
may utilize either procedure for De Novo classification.
    Under the first procedure, the person submits a premarket 
notification (510(k)) for a device that has not previously been 
classified. After receiving an order from FDA classifying the device 
into class III under section 513(f)(1) of the FD&C Act, the person then 
requests a classification under section 513(f)(2).
    Under the second procedure, rather than first submitting a 510(k) 
and then a request for classification, if the person determines that 
there is no legally marketed device upon which to base a determination 
of substantial equivalence, that person requests a classification under 
section 513(f)(2) of the FD&C Act.
    Under either procedure for De Novo classification, FDA is required 
to classify the device by written order within 120 days. The 
classification will be according to the criteria under section 
513(a)(1) of the FD&C Act. Although the device was automatically placed 
within class III, the De Novo classification is considered to be the 
initial classification of the device.
    We believe this De Novo classification will enhance patients' 
access to beneficial innovation, in part by reducing regulatory 
burdens. When FDA classifies a device into class I or II via the De 
Novo process, the device can serve as a predicate for future devices of 
that type, including for 510(k)s (see section 513(f)(2)(B)(i) of the 
FD&C Act). As a result, other device sponsors do not have to submit a 
De Novo request or premarket approval application to market a 
substantially equivalent device (see section 513(i) of the FD&C Act, 
defining ``substantial equivalence''). Instead, sponsors can use the 
less burdensome 510(k) process, when necessary, to market their device.

II. De Novo Classification

    On August 27, 2021, FDA received Hologic Inc.'s request for De Novo 
classification of the Genius Digital Diagnostics System with the Genius 
Cervical AI algorithm. FDA reviewed the request in order to classify 
the device under the criteria for classification set forth in section 
513(a)(1) of the FD&C Act.
    We classify devices into class II if general controls by themselves 
are insufficient to provide reasonable assurance of the safety and 
effectiveness of the device, but there is sufficient information to 
establish special controls that, in combination with the general 
controls, provide reasonable assurance of the safety and effectiveness 
of the device for its intended use (see section 513(a)(1)(B) of the 
FD&C Act). After review of the information submitted in the request, we 
determined that the device can be classified into class II with the 
establishment of special controls. FDA has determined that these 
special controls, in addition to the general controls, will provide 
reasonable assurance of the safety and effectiveness of the device.
    Therefore, on January 31, 2024, FDA issued an order to the 
requester classifying the device into class II. In this final order, 
FDA is codifying the classification of the device by adding 21 CFR 
864.3900.\1\ We have named the

[[Page 69688]]

generic type of device ``digital cervical cytology slide imaging system 
with artificial intelligence algorithm,'' and it is identified as a 
prescription in vitro diagnostic device consisting of an automated 
digital slide creation, viewing, and management system intended to aid 
in the review of digital images of slides prepared from Pap test 
specimens and conventional Pap smears by selecting and presenting areas 
of interest to facilitate interpretation by the reader. The artificial 
intelligence (AI) software algorithm uses machine learning techniques 
to provide information to the user about the presence, location, or 
characteristics of areas of the image with clinical implications.

Navy unfairly evaluated Saildrone MUSV proposal, court finds - Breaking Defense

Saildrone's new Spectre MUSV comes in two variants: The Spectre Silent Endurance and the Spectre Stealth Strike. (Saildrone)

PARIS — The US Navy unfairly evaluated maritime drone manufacturer Saildrone’s proposal for the service’s medium unmanned surface vessel (MUSV) program, according to a ruling from the US Court of Federal Claims.

As a result, the Navy must reevaluate Saildrone’s proposal within the next two months, and is barred from spending a large chunk of its MUSV budget until that process is complete.

Saildrone and maritime tech startup Blue Water Autonomy filed lawsuits in June challenging the Navy’s decision to eliminate their respective proposals — Saildrone’s Spectre and Blue Water Autonomy’s Liberty — from the MUSV competition. The companies argued that their platforms met the Navy’s requirements for the MUSV marketplace, which launched in March, and that the service didn’t stick to its own evaluation guidance in the request for proposals (RFP).

“The Court finds that the Navy engaged in disparate treatment, and thus, acted in an arbitrary and capricious manner in its review of Saildrone’s proposal,” Judge Philip Hadji wrote in his opinion, which was originally issued Oct. 30 and publicly released on Wednesday.

The Navy originally disqualified Saildrone from advancing to on-water testing due to discrepancies between the company’s proposal and a summary document known as a J-8 Placemat, which is related to the maximum displacement of the design. The opinion said the Navy “eliminated Saildrone because its Placemat reported loaded displacements exceeded the stated maximum displacement.”

However, the court determined that Saildrone received disparate treatment compared to other firms because the Navy advanced a proposal from Sea Machines despite similar issues involving maximum displacement. It’s unclear which Sea Machines vessel — either the Steamracer of the Steamrunner — the Navy evaluated, the opinion said. However, the court noted that the distinction did not affect its finding.

“Because the Navy accepted from Sea Machines a Placemat that either reported both payload-condition displacements above the stated ‘Max Displacement,’ as Saildrone’s did (STEAMRUNNER), or left those fields blank (STEAMRACER), the Court finds the Navy’s subsequent treatment of the proposals disparately favored Sea Machines and arbitrarily held Saildrone to a higher standard,” the opinion said.

presented by

Sponsored Post,

Land Warfare

#

Weaponizing the supply chain for a liquid-fueled howitzer-fired munition that flies 150 km

The goal of such weaponization is to tie warfighter needs to the RDT&E cycle.

By Breaking Defense

Under the ruling, the court ordered the Navy to reevaluate Saildrone’s proposal within 60 days, applying the same evaluation approach it used for companies that advanced in the competition. The ruling also prohibits the Navy from relying on its previously withdrawn findings under two other evaluation criteria to eliminate Saildrone.

The court also barred the Navy from spending more than $1.5 billion of the $2.1 billion allocated for the program on production until it completes that reevaluation.

A US Navy spokesperson told Breaking Defense that it will comply with the court’s order and reevaluate Saildrone’s proposal to determine if it will qualify for on-water testing.

“The future of naval warfare will be fought on the water, not in a courtroom,” Richard Jenkins, Saildrone’s founder and CEO, said in a statement on Monday. “We are eager to move beyond this litigation and return our entire focus to delivering world-leading maritime autonomy for the US Navy, to help secure America’s future maritime dominance. This ruling is a win for fair competition, for taxpayers, and for national security.”

# Blue Water Ruling

However, Hadji reached a different conclusion regarding Blue Water Autonomy, determining that “the Navy reasonably rated Blue Water unacceptable.”

The service eliminated the company from the competition for several reasons, including because it claimed that Blue Water’s test vessel — a twin-hulled catamaran — was not “representative” of its production vessel, an axe-bow monohull.

However, Blue Water Autonomy argued that the Navy deviated from its own evaluation requirements because “[h]ull and machinery plants are not listed as assets to be evaluated in the testing.”

The court disagreed, and the opinion said that “the Court concludes that ‘representative’ unambiguously calls for comparing the test vessel with the production vessel,” and noted that the solicitation did not exclude hull form or propulsion architecture from that comparison.

Even so, Austin Gray, co-founder and chief strategy officer at Blue Water Autonomy, said in a statement to Breaking Defense that “nothing about the test vessel was core to our technology, our ship, or our product.”

Gray also said the Navy has made positive changes in Phase II of its MUSV program the service unveiled in September.

For example, Phase I required proposals to travel 2,500 nautical miles at 25 knots in sea state 4 conditions with a payload capacity of two 40-foot containers. In contrast, Phase II requires that proposals include a payload capacity of at least two standard 20-foot shipping containers and eliminates the high-speed requirement.

“The Navy’s new leadership team has already leaned ahead and fixed problems highlighted by the protest,” Gray said. “The Medium USV Phase II program steers away from the prescriptive, compliance-centric testing rules of the previous competition, a change made by thoughtful Navy acquisition professionals months ago.”

Christopher Miller, Direct Reporting Portfolio Manager for robotic and autonomous systems (DRPM RAS) recently acknowledged some difficulties that Phase I requirements presented for industry. He said the Navy wants to “open the aperture” for new entrants and increase options for other services that may be interested in the capabilities.

Shield AI cofounder teases 'snowball' of X-BAT fighter drone announcements in Europe - Breaking Defense






ShieldAI's first full-scale prototype of the X-Bat drone. (ShieldAI)

MUNICH — A “snowball of activities” covering European orders and regional partnership agreements for Shield AI’s X-BAT fighter jet drone are set to be announced “soon,” according to the company’s cofounder and chief strategy officer.

Speaking to Breaking Defense today on the sidelines of the International Fighter Conference, Ryan Tseng said that the prospective deals and new industry pacts will be publicized when “we’re ready to announce them.”

He declined to comment on any aircraft quantities involved in the procurements, saying just “watch this space.”

Europe “can and should be a critical component of the [X-BAT] supply chain for Europe,” he said, noting it would make the region stronger at a “warfighting” level. Additionally, a “European sovereign” supply chain, makes the US more capable, stressed Tseng.

Andrew Hawkes, X-BAT director for Europe at Shield AI, also told Breaking Defense that the company is involved in “several active” sales campaigns for the autonomous, vertical takeoff and landing (VTOL) aircraft across the continent, though he declined to disclose any individual customers.

The planned export business builds on a number of other key, regional developments. In June, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk reportedly said that Shield AI was planning local production of X-BAT in cooperation with Poland. More recently, the firm announced a “strategic agreement” with Greece’s GEK TERNA, a critical infrastructure investor, based on a potential collaboration on “parts production, aircraft integration and long-term sustainment for X-BAT in Greece .”

Tseng’s assessment of orders comes after the artificial intelligence startup announced on Tuesday that a first, full-scale X-BAT prototype has completed assembly in Frisco, Texas. Next steps will see the aircraft undergo testing at the company’s facility in Newton, Kan., according to a company statement. Shield AI and the US Navy are jointly investing $400 million in X-BAT.

Elsewhere, Tseng said that the per-aircraft cost for the autonomous drone could be brought down to $25 million, but for a higher-end sensor configuration, customers could expect to pay an extra $10 million.

The baseline $25 million figure works out to around one-quarter “the cost of a Eurofighter or an F-35 in Europe,” he explained. “We think from a lifecycle perspective, it would beat it [in production fighter jets] by a factor of 10″ based on comparable maintenance costs. “You can use far less crew to operate the aircraft” resulting in “savings across the board.”

It describes a policy blueprint in which the company will not use non-disclosure agreements with public officials, except narrow protections for legitimate security information, trade secrets, or competitively sensitive information. On electricity, it commits to pay the full cost of the electricity it uses and the infrastructure needed to serve it. For residents, it says it will engage residents early enough for their input to shape project plans, provide a local point of contact, and report publicly each year.

Related reporting on the Stargate sites adds context. Reuters reported that each Stargate site will get its own locally tailored community plan, "driven by community input and local concerns," OpenAI said. The concerns behind these commitments are real. One report said new AI centers have drawn resident anger for driving up household electricity bills in at least 13 states. Brookings urged AI companies to establish viable community benefit agreements to address public concerns.

Caveats: the search didn't turn up independent verification of how OpenAI applies the NDA policy or whether the electricity pledges have been enforced. Some results were aggregator sites (MEXC, Yahoo reposts), so the OpenAI post and the Reuters and Bloomberg pieces are the more reliable sources. # OpenAI kicks off charm offensive to change voters' view of data centers

By Deepa Seetharaman
Thu, November 5, 2026 at 4:04 AM CST 3 min read

- OPAI.PVT

By Deepa Seetharaman
SAN FRANCISCO, Nov 5 (Reuters) - Stunning victories by Democrats in US midterm elections this week have been interpreted by many as Americans repudiating tech industry plans to build data centers across the country. OpenAI ‌has now embarked on new strategies to change their minds.

The AI lab on Thursday laid out policies — in the ‌works since August — intended to help the company build more trust with local communities and convince them that data centers will benefit them.
OpenAI said it will ​no longer use non-disclosure agreements with public officials when negotiating or discussing future sites, although proprietary information would still be under wraps. It will also give residents access to construction plans and their potential effect on traffic, noise and lighting.
OpenAI's chief global affairs officer Chris Lehane also said that these centers would be a source of ongoing jobs because the hardware within the data center would ‌need to be updated every three to five ⁠years.
"These projects are not the types of data centers that people have historically thought about, which are some version of a black box in a pasture that did very little in terms of ⁠the economic utility for the communities they were in," he told reporters.

One OpenAI facility in southern Ohio is expected to create 2,500 long-term jobs with an average annual salary of $80,000, he said.
Partners such as Oracle are building and own much of OpenAI's data center infrastructure, ​with the ​capacity dedicated to the startup.
DATA CENTER OPPONENTS MAKE BIG GAINS
In some ​of the biggest upsets of the elections, Democrats flipped ‌governorships in Texas, Georgia and Ohio with candidates who have promised to pause new data center permits and tighten construction rules.
And of the 41 data center-related ballot measures voted on this week, all but one went against data centers, according to Ballotpedia.
Shares of data center operators and power companies that have been among the biggest beneficiaries of the AI building boom also tumbled on Wednesday as investors bet the Democratic sweep could bring tougher permitting, higher costs and a slower pace of construction.
"We need to ‌do a better job of really communicating to people, to local communities, ​about why data centers can be beneficial to them," OpenAI President Greg ​Brockman said at a separate event on Wednesday.

OpenAI officials, ​along with many of their peers in tech, have spent the last two years trying to build ‌ties with the administration of US President Donald ​Trump in hopes of shaping federal ​policy around AI.

Story Continues
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman donated $1 million to Trump's inaugural committee and later attended Trump's second inauguration. Last year, Brockman donated $25 million in his personal capacity to a Trump super PAC.
When asked about how the company would address ​skepticism from some Democrats, Lehane pointed to ‌his extensive experience in the party. During the Clinton administration, he served as a top lawyer and spokesperson ​and he was also press secretary for Vice President Al Gore when he made his run for ​president.
(Reporting by Deepa Seetharaman in San Francisco; Editing by Edwina Gibbs)

42:Qwen 3.8 27B on my laptop can interpret model weights, too 2026-11-03T16:29:48+00:00 2026-11-03T16:29:48+00:00 https://simonwillison.net/2026/Nov/3/qwen-can-interpret-model-weights/ 43:

Yesterday's hot paper was Sparks of Weight-Space Programming: LLMs can natively read & write neural network weights by Rikiya Takehi, Jayden Teoh, Alex Zhang, and Omar Khattab. The paper (OK, the authors classify is as a "blog post", but it's paper-shaped) found that frontier models, in particular GPT-6 Astra, can both interpret and modify the raw weights of a machine learning model - literally a text description of the model containing a bunch of floating point numbers. I've been playing with one of the examples from the paper and I'm delighted to share that Qwen 3.8 27B running on my laptop can do this as well!

48:

Likewise, asked to make Qwen3.5-0.8B better at math without gradients, Astra identifies an issue in its weights causing reasoning loops that Qwen’s own model card warns about, and fixes this by natively editing 0.016% of the weights. With the same sampling settings, this weight correction raises MATH-500 from 7.9% to 48.1% and generalizes out of the box to instruction following, raising IFEval by 3x.

52:

spaCy author Matthew Honnibal called the paper misleading for conflating the two, and Sean Goedecke deconstructed the Qwen3.5-0.8B update example as taking the same steps that a human ML researcher would use.

54:

The paper presents the first question as Can LLMs understand model behaviors from weights? content.title: A thousand fewer paths to root
948 Linux Root Exploits in One Run: What OpenAI's Kernel Pipeline Actually Proves — and What It Doesn't - DEV Community
A thousand fewer paths to root
OpenAI Agents Found 948 Linux Root Exploits for $1.2M

results:
OpenAI's November 4, 2026 report, "A thousand fewer paths to root," describes an autonomous pipeline that produced 948 Linux kernel local privilege-escalation exploits. Coverage is consistent on the headline number, though some details differ across secondary sources.

- **Funnel:** The prototype identified and analyzed 2,308 candidate Linux kernel findings, dynamically reproduced 1,724 vulnerabilities, and produced 948 local privilege escalation (LPE) exploits. Validation ran in an isolated virtual machine running a Linux kernel with Kernel Address Sanitizer (KASAN).
- **Model and timing:** The run used an upcoming cyber model against the kernel's master branch in mid-October.
- **Cost:** Sources cite $1,213,430 in API credits end to end.
- **Definition of 948:** One source notes that the 948 is the count of unique LPEs, defined by the distinct patch that closes each one — not a count of merged kernel fixes.
- **Early error:** Initially, the agents reported 200 working root exploits. However, 20 of them actually gained root by triggering a different zero-day bug than the one assigned.
- **Patch status:** One source reports that 61 LPEs had already been patched upstream, 43 had staging patches, and 299 were being reported and discussed publicly, but this figure is from a secondary blog, not the OpenAI post itself. Another notes that the public summary does not say how many patches were ultimately accepted.
- **Side findings:** When analysts sampled 166 exploits from the run, they found 10 new Linux exploit tricks. The run also produced 291 information-leak proofs of concept.

Caveat: most results are secondary coverage and blogs, and some of their figures (such as the "$1.2M" rounding and the patch-status counts) should be checked against OpenAI's original post.

response.result:
**What Conductor does:** Its software lets a developer run several coding agents at once, each in an isolated copy of the codebase, then review and merge what they produce. The desktop app runs on Macs. Conductor Cloud runs agents in sandboxed virtual machines, and an iPhone app lets users check on them.

**User count:** Conductor's website says "more than 100,000 people use it."

**Deal terms:** Meta Platforms acquired Conductor, according to a deal first reported by Axios. Terms were not disclosed.

**Supported agents and their makers:**
- Claude Code, made by Anthropic PBC
- Codex, made by OpenAI Group PBC
- Cursor, made by Space Exploration Technologies Corp.

Users pay for these agents through their own subscriptions and keys.

**Shutdown timeline:**
- **Nov. 4, 2026 (today):** New sign-ups and downloads are halted. Pro subscribers get their paid features free.
- **Nov. 13:** The cloud service goes read-only.
- **Nov. 20:** The cloud service shuts down. The company will then start deleting stored cloud data.
- **Before Nov. 20:** Users can export their data or move cloud workspaces onto their own machines. Active subscribers will get refunds.
- **Early 2027:** Local Mac app copies stop receiving new models and critical bug fixes, and Conductor will delete the app's user data. The team expects to release a new interface by then, which it has not yet described.

**Who the team will work with at Meta:** The article does not name specific Meta teams or leaders. It says people familiar with the deal told Axios that Meta expects the Conductor team's shipping speed to help it build its next generation of AI coding tools.

**Publication date and time:** The page is dated November 4, 2026. The timestamp shown is "UPDATED 17:20 EST / NOVEMBER 04 2026," which is the last update time. The original publication time is not shown.

**What it is:** An Anthropic Frontier Red Team post, published **Nov 2, 2026**, on "provable inference" for large language models. It describes zkSNARK-based cryptographic proofs that let a user check a response came from a committed model, and it introduces **FlashProve**, which it calls "an open-source performant prototype for provable inference." The post also releases code, Lean proofs, and a technical report under Apache 2.0.

**Key figures (Llama 4 Maverick, 400B-parameter MoE, 4-bit weights, one H100):**

- Proof generation: "a single H100 GPU generates proofs at around 110 tokens/second"
- Proof size: "with a proof size of ~19 MB per 1,024-token request"
- Overhead: "This is ~70-95x the GPU time of running the model itself on vLLM"
- Offline commitment: "takes about 39 minutes."
- Online phase: "takes the prover about 223 seconds" for a batch of 24 requests, and "each proof is 18.78 MB"
- Commitment validity: "the resulting commitment is good for about 16 million requests"
- Verifier: "Checking a proof takes 17 seconds on 24 threads" and "(and 21 seconds on a single thread)"
- Client download: "~6.5 MB in all"
- vs. vLLM (FP8, eight H100s): "about 72 times longer than vLLM takes to process the same 24 requests at once," with "66 to 77 across runs," and "about 94 times longer when vLLM runs at the highest load we tried"

**Limitations noted:** The proof covers an integer version of the weights under greedy decoding, not sampled or floating-point output. Architecture is not hidden. Side-channel attacks are out of scope. Context is limited to 1,024 tokens.

results:
Moonshot AI has published the Kimi K3.1 Pro open weights on Hugging Face, and the sources agree on the core facts, though they differ on dates and licensing.

- **Release:** The weights are in the public repository moonshotai/Kimi-K3.1-Pro. Moonshot AI completed the promise it made at launch on 4 November 2026. One report dates the Hugging Face upload to November 5 instead, so the exact day depends on the source.
- **Not a new model:** The model itself came earlier. K3.1 Pro launched 23 October 2026; today completes the promised open-weights step.
- **Architecture:** It is a 2.8T-parameter mixture-of-experts model with 104 billion active per token and a 1M-token context window. One source adds that it accepts text and image input.
- **Benchmarks:** Moonshot says it is close to the top closed models on coding. One report says it comes within a point of Claude Opus 5.5 on coding. Another notes that Moonshot's coding comparisons do not establish a general advantage, and Kimi trails Claude Opus 5.5 on some tests. Arena's Agent Arena leaderboard reportedly ranks it first among open-weight models.
- **Safety:** Moonshot removed cyberattack-related material from training before the open release.
- **License:** Sources disagree. One describes the Kimi K3.1-Pro License as MIT-style, custom. Another says Kimi K3 uses a custom, non-OSI-approved license, so teams should verify commercial use, modification, and redistribution terms in the repository before deployment. Check the repository license before commercial use.

What the New AI Training Opt-Out Really Means | TechPolicy.Press Perspective

# What the New AI Training Opt-Out Really Means
Alissa Cooper / Nov 4, 2026 Alissa Cooper is the executive director of the Knight-Georgetown Institute (KGI).
Primitive Accumulation by Daniela Zampieri / Better Images of AI / CC by 4.0

Republish

Share

Last week, Google , Microsoft , Anthropic , and OpenAI all announced plans to support a new mechanism that lets web publishers express their desire to opt out of having their content used to train AI models. The proposal , authored by Anthropic’s Kevin Kelley, attracted considerable attention across the tech press (see here and here ) and on social media , with the coverage highlighting the prospect of giving publishers greater control over how AI companies use their content.
But the announcements — and much of the subsequent coverage — leave out important context about the relationship between the product changes, ongoing standardization activity, and the policy environment. Understanding these nuances requires looking at the ongoing standards process and the broader policy debates surrounding AI, search, and competition.
The new proposal comes after years of disputes between publishers and companies that crawl the web — in court rooms, industry standards bodies, and public forums. Nearly two years ago, the Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF), the premier internet standards development organization, launched an effort known as AI Preferences (“AIPREF”) to develop new standards that would, among other things, give websites expanded options for automatically expressing preferences about how their content gets used for AI-related purposes. This work is meant to build in part on a prior IETF standard, RFC 9309: Robots Exclusion Protocol , which specifies the format for the commonly used “robots.txt” files employed by websites to control crawlers. Participants from Anthropic, Google, and Microsoft have all been actively involved in the AIPREF group, while OpenAI contributions have been minimal, despite the company stating last week that the announcement “strengthens our continued participation in the IETF standards discussions.”
This AIPREF work was sparked in part by the process of developing the EU General-Purpose AI Code of Practice , a voluntary compliance mechanism under the EU AI Act. Is signatories (most of the largest American and European AI model companies) commit to abide by the machine-readable preferences that sites express.
When looking beyond the headlines, what’s most important to understand about these announcements?

# 1. The mechanism is not an official “standard” — but adoption by the four largest search and AI providers might make it a de facto one.
Last week’s proposal has no official status in the IETF. It will need to be discussed and debated (probably at some length) to see if it will move forward toward standardization. But when the largest companies deploy support for it (all have committed to do so by 2027), that standardization status may not matter. If site operators are convinced to change their robots.txt files to comply with the new proposal, it may become the de facto way of signaling AI training preferences regardless of where the standards end up.
The proposal announced on October 30 (the “policy token draft,” for short) is documented in what is colloquially known as an “individual draft” — a submission to the IETF made by an author, which has no formal standing of any kind in the standards process. Anyone can submit an individual draft to the IETF, and over 1,000 are submitted each year.
The AIPREF working group already has two other drafts that are further along in the standards process, one that expresses a vocabulary for AI-related preferences (the “vocabulary draft ”) and one that specifies how those preferences could be expressed in the widely used robots.txt files that many websites already publish (the “attachment draft ”). In IETF parlance, these two drafts have been “adopted” by the AIPREF working group, which means the participants in the working group had rough consensus to pursue those approaches to meet the working group’s goals.
The policy token draft has no such consensus since it’s one individual’s submission that has not yet been considered by the group. After discussion, the group may or may not adopt it or integrate its contents into the attachment draft.

# 2. A training preference is nice to have, but a search-specific preference is missing, while the spotlight in the industry has shifted to inference.
Much of the discussion in the AIPREF working group over the last two years has centered on the definitions of new AI-related preferences in the vocabulary draft. These definitions matter because they are the categories for which sites will be able to express preferences in their robots.txt files (and via other technical mechanisms).

After significant discussion, the group has made progress towards settling on a definition of “AI training,” although discussions of some wording remain ongoing. After significantly more (and more heated) discussion, a definition of what it means for website content to be used in “search” has also been (mostly) provisionally agreed. Both definitions saw updates and new text added after the working group met in person at the end of August. Contentious discussions about a broader and more amorphous category — which has variously tried to cover “AI use,” “inference,” “grounding,” and related uses that occur separate from model training — are ongoing.
The policy token draft specifically leverages the “AI training” definition from the vocabulary draft and proposes a way that sites could express a preference to disallow all AI training, across all crawlers, by adding a few simple lines to their existing robots.txt files. The attachment draft already contains a similar mechanism, but the advantage of the approach in the policy token draft is that it would more immediately be machine-readable by many crawlers that are already deployed. This is the key value of the approach in the policy token draft: for site owners suffering from having to constantly update an ever-growing list of crawlers that they individually disallow, the newly proposed mechanism offers the prospect of a single, simple solution to express a preference to disallow all crawlers from AI training.
But what about search uses? And inference-time uses more broadly?
It is notable that the policy token draft does not provide an equivalent mechanism to cover search, especially given that the two companies that represent almost the entire web search market have signed up already to support it. It could have been quite powerful and clarifying for them to send the message that they want to make “search: yes; AI training: no” simple for sites to declare. The search definition in the vocabulary draft could have been leveraged in the same way that the AI training definition was. Publishers’ inability to express search-specific preferences has been the subject of regulatory investigation and intervention across multiple jurisdictions, making this omission all the more striking.
The new proposal’s focus on training also reinforces the difficult line-drawing that is still to come around inference-time uses more broadly. While the AIPREF working group has churned through multiple attempts at defining an inference or “AI usage” category, consensus has remained elusive, even as negotiation of licensing deals has shifted towards inference and recurring revenue. Microsoft’s announcement indicated that the company will combine support for the policy token mechanism with its own company-specific grounding preference mechanism, demonstrating the need for preference signals that go beyond training.

# 3. Since the mechanism has yet to be standardized, signatories to the EU AI Act Code of Practice are not required to commit to recognizing it.
Google’s announcement stated that the proposed mechanism is “consistent with the EU Code of Practice for General Purpose AI (GPAI) Model Providers under the EU AI Act.” Yet the text of the Code of Practice is clear that it commits signatories to follow standardized crawler instructions only:
Signatories commit … to employ web-crawlers that read and follow instructions expressed in accordance with the Robot Exclusion Protocol (robots.txt), as specified in the Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF) Request for Comments No. 9309, and any subsequent version of this Protocol for which the IETF demonstrates that it is technically feasible and implementable by AI providers and content providers, including rightsholders
As noted above, with the policy token draft having been published less than a week ago, it has a ways to go before being formally standardized, extending RFC 9309, or demonstrating technical feasibility. As much as all involved surely want a speedy resolution, giving interested stakeholders a chance to review and debate the mechanism’s design is a critical part of the process that helps yield stronger standards that are more easily deployable and (hopefully) meet the needs of more website owners.

# Conclusion
A common mechanism supported by the largest AI and search providers could substantially reduce the burden on publishers who must currently manage crawler rules one crawler at a time. But it is important to be clear about the limitations of what has been announced: the preference applies only to AI training, leaving out search and other inference-time uses. As an individual draft, it has many steps to go before formal standardization, during which time its design could change significantly. That process should be allowed to run before a few of the world’s largest companies decide the rules for the wider web to have to follow.

Tim Hua 13h * 21
