Large language models (LLMs) are evolving from passive scientific assistants into agents that take on parts of the research process. When equipped with external tools, these agents can search and summarize literature, formulate hypotheses, write and debug scientific code, and produce technical reports. Recent systems have demonstrated tool-augmented reasoning in chemistry, iterative code-based experimentation, multi-agent hypothesis generation, scientific-software optimization, and even interaction with laboratory instruments [ 30 , 6 , 29 , 37 , 17 , 4 , 33 , 41 , 20 , 22 , 18 , 31 , 15 ] . These systems point toward agents that contribute to more complete scientific workflows and projects, not only isolated subtasks [ 9 ] .
Evaluating progress toward this goal requires benchmarks that capture the open-ended, multi-stage nature of scientific research. Scientific benchmarks are accordingly shifting from textbook-level questions [ 16 , 23 , 48 , 35 , 44 ] toward expert-level closed-ended questions [ 8 ] and research-level problems [ 40 ] . Among existing research-level benchmarks, some assess scientific reasoning [ 10 , 50 , 34 , 25 , 46 ] , while others evaluate the agents’ ability to complete individual tasks within realistic scientific workflows [ 43 , 19 , 31 , 28 , 7 , 21 ] . However, these benchmarks target isolated capabilities, and because many of their tasks are closed-ended with deterministic answers, models quickly saturate them, so the benchmarks lose signal. To move toward end-to-end research, some benchmarks formulate tasks as full-paper reproductions [ 36 , 12 , 49 , 14 ] . Yet because agents are given the original publications, the research questions and solution structures are largely specified in advance, limiting their ability to evaluate open-ended scientific inquiry. More recent benchmarks address this limitation by converting published studies into research problems without revealing their solutions [ 32 , 45 , 47 , 24 ] . Nevertheless, designing and evaluating such tasks involves many subtleties that require the expertise of the original authors: for example, how to write instructions that preserve as much open-endedness as possible while avoiding false negatives, and how to determine if an agent’s failure reflects true scientific misunderstanding or a lack of expert intuition and experience. To our knowledge, no existing benchmark is fully agentic, built by physicists from their own research, graded on both paper quality and result correctness, and designed to address these subtleties through manual task review and failure-mode analysis (Table 1 ).
We compare scientific research benchmarks across the research authenticity, research components covered in the evaluation, and the evaluation methods. Meanings of labels: Tasks/Phys. : total/physics task counts in released task lists. Own Research : the tasks come from the contributors’ own research. No Reference Given : there is no reference (e.g., the original paper) provided to the agent. Literature Graded : the quality of agents’ literature review and synthesis is evaluated. Write-up Graded : agents write up scientific manuscripts and the manuscripts are graded. Expert Rubric : at least part of the evaluation protocol uses rubrics created by domain experts. Deterministic Verifiers : at least part of the evaluation protocol contains deterministic verifiers. Failure Analysis : domain experts manually check the trajectories and output papers of selected rollouts.
Each task requires two types of final deliverables: deterministic artifacts, such as computed quantities, simulation outputs, or processed data, and a paper manuscript submitted as paper.pdf . The paper is expected to meet the standards of a peer-reviewed paper by clearly presenting the research context, methodology, results, and conclusions, while faithfully incorporating the evidence and computational artifacts produced during task execution.
We evaluate 22 frontier models in four agent harnesses. Each model attempts all 56 tasks three times at its highest available inference effort, and four GPT models are also run at xhigh.
Figure 4: Task composition and overall pass rate (%) by primary physics domain across all 56 tasks. Donut labels give task shares. n n gives task counts.
Table 2: Detailed Frontier-model performance across all 56 tasks. For the experiment we use the highest available inference effort by default, where configurable. GPT models also appear at xhigh. The Score column reports the score defined in Equation 1 , averaged over the three rollouts for each task and then across all tasks. Deterministic pass requires all verifier tests to pass and overall pass additionally requires all blocking rubric criteria to pass. Pass@1 gives the average pass rate over the three rollouts, while Pass@3 gives the percentage of tasks with at least one passing rollout. Uncertainties are approximate 95% binomial confidence intervals over all rollouts, as in Figure FrontierPhysics: Evaluating Agents for
Verifier and rubric defects may remain after review. One major source of defects is adversarial verifier or rubric engineering designed to suppress task pass rates, such that even correct solutions produced by human experts may fail. To mitigate this, we have a three stage process:
First, we ask every task contributor to do a failure-mode report of the three GPT-6 Astra rollouts, as this is the best performing model with single agent harness when the analysis started, check the agent trajectories and output files, and explain where the agent failed and why. Second, our admin team reviewers re-read these contributors’ failure-mode reports and double check them against the agent trajectories and output files. After reviewing around 60 rollouts, reviewers consolidated the recurring failures into the taxonomy in Table 4 . False negatives, where agents deliver the correct results but failed by verifier or reviewer agent, are found during this process and are labeled in Appendix E . As highlighted in Table 5 , rollouts with exclusively false failures lead to an underestimated pass rate. In total, nine of the 168 rollouts incorrectly failed.
The non-blocking rubric scores are harder to assess because they involve more subjective judgments. Third, as a sanity check of the rubric quality we asked authors to include their own papers or manuscripts as reference materials in the oracle when possible. Thirty-three tasks included these materials. For those with available reference, we selected the manuscript-level rubric criteria used for grading these materials, including blocker and non-blocker scoring criteria against the authors’ reference work. We then use the same configuration as main experiment to run reviewer agents in sandboxes to grade these files with rubrics. The authors’ own materials score 96.2% on average under corresponding rubrics (Table 11 ), showing good alignment between rubrics grading with the human expert materials.
To find why agents fail and how well the agent score approximates what we want to measure, we follow the protocol of Section 3.3 . Figure 6 summarizes the earlier matched-cohort annotations for all 168 single agent GPT-6 Astra rollouts. Table 5 reports the final review-sheet labels. More detailed information and an explanation of the failure modes can be found in Table 4 . This process found design issues in some tasks. We fixed them and re-ran or regraded the affected results (Section 3.1 ). The pass rate of GPT-6 Astra (xhigh) after the re-runs (Table 2 ) agrees well with the manually corrected pass rate in Figure 6 .
Figure 6: Failure mode analysis of GPT-6 Astra xhigh across 56 tasks (3 rollouts for each task). Counts n n and percentages ( n / 143 n/143 ) use the final review labels in Table 5 . Each rollout may have multiple tags. Verifier/rubric proportions are retained from the original recorded assessment. Correcting the eight FALSE and one RRMIS outcomes changes the pass rate from 14.9% (25/168) to 20.2% (34/168).
We have introduced FrontierPhysics , a benchmark dataset with 56 tasks evaluating the ability of AI agents to conduct physics research across nine domains. FrontierPhysics shows end-to-end physics research remains challenging to current models, given that Opus 5.5 in Claude Code CLI, the configuration with the highest pass rate, passes only 46 of its 168 rollouts. Based on the human experts auditing of 168 SOTA agents rollouts trajectory and output files, we build a failure mode taxonomy and label all these 168 rollouts manually. From the taxonomy distribution, we conclude that lack of rigorous thinking (for example, circular self-verification) followed by missing expert intuition, instead of insufficient physics knowledge or execution mistakes, are the main weaknesses of frontier LLM agents.

AI Agents are becoming digital coworkers that can browse the web, write code, run experiments, and assist humans over extended horizons. Yet existing benchmarks fall short of real knowledge work: many rely on synthetic data or isolated tasks, missing the complex, multi-party dynamics of collaborative projects, where critical information is scattered across conversations, code, and evolving decisions. Even simple workplace questions may require locating relevant channels and direct messages, recovering context from long discussions, inspecting repository state, reconciling stale or conflicting evidence, and synthesizing across sources.
We introduce SlackBench, a benchmark for evaluating agents on realistic research and engineering workflows that require joint reasoning over workplace communication and evolving repository state. Grounded in privacy-preserving reenactments of real academic research projects, SlackBench provides reproducible environments with realistic multi-party dialogue, evolving decisions, and corresponding code changes grounded in GitHub repositories and Google Docs. It contains 140 queries spanning heterogeneous-source agentic search, abstention on unanswerable or false-premise questions, goal-directed summarization, and circumstance inference over long conversations. These tasks are not reducible to static corpus question answering: agents must determine which conversations matter, traverse threads, inspect repository state, and synthesize evidence across communication and code artifacts. Across 33 frontier models and agent harnesses, the best system scores around 80% and most agents score below 66%, highlighting substantial headroom for improvement. SlackBench thus provides an extensible framework for evaluating agents in collaborative work environments.

Large language model agents are increasingly positioned as digital coworkers that can write code, run experiments, interact with diverse workplace applications, browse the web, and assist humans over extended horizons. Yet the benchmarks used to measure this progress still capture only fragments of real knowledge work. In practice, project state is scattered across Slack channels, Google Docs, GitHub commits, source files, experiment outputs, and informal decisions that evolve over time. Answering a seemingly simple workplace question often requires deciding where to look, recovering context from long multi-party discussions, reconciling stale or conflicting statements, inspecting the codebase, browsing the web, and synthesizing evidence across all of these sources.
Existing evaluation suites have improved realism for web navigation, software engineering, workplace simulation, and long-horizon memory ( Wei et al., 2025 ; Jimenez et al., 2024 ) , but they typically isolate only one or two components of this process. On the other hand, benchmarks that study agents in multi-platform professional settings rarely combine heterogeneous workplace applications with conversations grounded in realistic collaborative scenarios, evolving decisions, and concrete project artifacts ( Xu et al., 2025 ; Deshpande et al., 2025 ) . We therefore lack a shareable and reproducible benchmark of grounded collaborative workspaces in which agents must reason across communication, documents, code, and repository history. results:
Super Micro reported fiscal first-quarter 2027 results on November 4, 2026, beating expectations and raising its full-year outlook. The results don't break out AI server revenue separately, so I can't confirm a specific AI-server figure.

- **Quarter:** Revenue was about $19.9 billion, up roughly 297% year over year, and above the company's own preliminary range. Non-GAAP EPS was $1.81 against about $1.23 expected. Super Micro Computer reported fiscal first-quarter revenue of $19.95 billion, up about 297% year over year and above both analyst estimates and its own preliminary range, with non-GAAP earnings of $1.81 per share.
- **Margins:** A non-GAAP diluted EPS of $1.81 and a non-GAAP gross margin of 12.8% exceeded forecasts and internal guidance.
- **Full-year guidance:** Fiscal 2027 revenue guidance was raised to $72–82 billion, up from the prior $65–72 billion. Full-year Revenue Guidance | $72–$82 billion | $65–$72 billion (prior)
- **Next quarter:** Q2 revenue guidance is $19.5–21.5 billion, with adjusted EPS of $1.66–1.90. Analyst consensus was reported at about $17.5 billion for revenue and $1.14 for EPS, though sources differ on the exact consensus figure.
- **Stock reaction:** Shares rose about 7% in extended and pre-market trading.

Some sources conflict. A Yahoo Finance piece covers the earlier fiscal 2026 Q4 report, with fiscal 2027 guidance of $65–72 billion, which predates the November update. Consensus figures also vary across outlets (for example, $17.4 billion, $17.51 billion, and $18.11 billion). Check the company's investor relations release for the official numbers.

AI agents are playing an increasingly important role in physics research. However, existing physics benchmarks only evaluate fixed questions, isolated sub-tasks, or paper reproduction with given solutions, and rarely check research quality alongside correctness. We introduce FrontierPhysics , an end-to-end benchmark with 56 tasks made by 42 physicists based on their own research, covering nine domains across theoretical, computational, and experimental physics. Each task requires agents to review the literature, develop a research plan, conduct research and experiments, and produce structured outputs and scientific manuscripts. Combining deterministic verifiers with expert-authored rubrics, FrontierPhysics evaluates whether agents’ research is correct and publishable. Across 22 models in 26 configurations, no configuration passes more than 46 of its 168 rollouts. Manual review of agent trajectories shows that frontier agents’ main weaknesses are insufficiently rigorous reasoning and limited expert intuition, rather than gaps in physics knowledge or execution errors.
Additionally, to keep the simulation close to real-world scenarios, we use both direct system prompting and subtle in-context prompting to control the non-coding behavior of the agents, including Slack messaging and GitHub operations. With direct system prompting, we instruct the model to communicate like a human research assistant and to follow a specified workflow when prompted. However, such workflows can be rigid and fail to capture the diverse conversational dynamics of a real research group. To mitigate this, we additionally embed subtle hints in the user prompts within the agent’s interactive interface to guide the conversation flow more naturally.
Affiliation: Stanford University
All our experiments are conducted using the Harbor framework ( Harbor Framework Team, 2026 ) . Specifically, we provide the agents with 2 sets of read-only tools: (1) SlackBench tools that we implement ourselves based on the official Slack Web API methods to search users, list channel history, search messages, etc. (2) GitHub tools to search any publicly available repository. We provide details for each tool in \cref tab:mcp_tools. We also enable the terminal read, bash, and web search tools for each agent. We give an illustration of agent trajectory in \cref fig:trajectory_show.
Concretely, as shown in \cref fig:slackbench, each channel in our Slack workspace corresponds to a real research project initiated from scratch around a concrete research idea (e.g., investigating the sensitivity of LLM tool-call accuracy to prompt format, as part of the Berkeley Function-Calling Leaderboard ( Patil et al., 2025 ) ). Conversations are produced by having humans and coding agents such as Cursor and Claude Code carry out—and in some cases complete—these research projects, using Slack as the primary communication platform. Humans play the role of project leads, while multiple agent sessions act as research assistants reporting to them. We create a Slack account and a GitHub account for each agent session and connect the agent to Slack and GitHub MCP servers ( Anthropic, 2024 ) .
Each task requires two types of final deliverables: deterministic artifacts, such as computed quantities, simulation outputs, or processed data, and a paper manuscript submitted as paper.pdf . The paper is expected to meet the standards of a peer-reviewed paper by clearly presenting the research context, methodology, results, and conclusions, while faithfully incorporating the evidence and computational artifacts produced during task execution.
Evaluating progress toward this goal requires benchmarks that capture the open-ended, multi-stage nature of scientific research. Scientific benchmarks are accordingly shifting from textbook-level questions [ 16 , 23 , 48 , 35 , 44 ] toward expert-level closed-ended questions [ 8 ] and research-level problems [ 40 ] . Among existing research-level benchmarks, some assess scientific reasoning [ 10 , 50 , 34 , 25 , 46 ] , while others evaluate the agents’ ability to complete individual tasks within realistic scientific workflows [ 43 , 19 , 31 , 28 , 7 , 21 ] . However, these benchmarks target isolated capabilities, and because many of their tasks are closed-ended with deterministic answers, models quickly saturate them, so the benchmarks lose signal. To move toward end-to-end research, some benchmarks formulate tasks as full-paper reproductions [ 36 , 12 , 49 , 14 ] . Yet because agents are given the original publications, the research questions and solution structures are largely specified in advance, limiting their ability to evaluate open-ended scientific inquiry. More recent benchmarks address this limitation by converting published studies into research problems without revealing their solutions [ 32 , 45 , 47 , 24 ] . Nevertheless, designing and evaluating such tasks involves many subtleties that require the expertise of the original authors: for example, how to write instructions that preserve as much open-endedness as possible while avoiding false negatives, and how to determine if an agent’s failure reflects true scientific misunderstanding or a lack of expert intuition and experience. To our knowledge, no existing benchmark is fully agentic, built by physicists from their own research, graded on both paper quality and result correctness, and designed to address these subtleties through manual task review and failure-mode analysis (Table 1 ).

Large language model agents are increasingly positioned as digital coworkers that can write code, run experiments, interact with diverse workplace applications, browse the web, and assist humans over extended horizons. Yet the benchmarks used to measure this progress still capture only fragments of real knowledge work. In practice, project state is scattered across Slack channels, Google Docs, GitHub commits, source files, experiment outputs, and informal decisions that evolve over time. Answering a seemingly simple workplace question often requires deciding where to look, recovering context from long multi-party discussions, reconciling stale or conflicting statements, inspecting the codebase, browsing the web, and synthesizing evidence across all of these sources.
Limits of AI for Scientific Discovery , 2025c.
Manipulation can depend on information that is no longer visible: an object’s identity before it is covered, the order of a demonstrated sequence, or the number of repetitions already completed. RoboMME [ 3 ] tests these dependencies with 16 tasks in four suites: Counting, Permanence, Reference, and Imitation. A common design for such tasks is hierarchical, with a vision-language model (VLM) choosing the next subtask and a vision-language-action (VLA) policy executing it.
Pick the requested cube ONCE, then keep holding it through the requested repetitions. Each back-and-forth repetition visits the RIGHT target and then the LEFT target, in that order. A completed right visit is half a repetition. After the final left visit, put the cube on the table, then press the button. Even if an instruction omits the intermediate release, use the standard put-down subgoal before pressing. The labels left/right use ROBOT perspective: in the fixed front image, robot-right is image-left and robot-left is image-right. Ground the target surface center, not an elevated gripper location. Repeated visits use their own ordinal within each side.
Similar to Choubey et al. (2025) , this category tests the information-seeking and deep-search capabilities of agents on real-world heterogeneous data. The agent may need to search across multiple Slack channels, GitHub repositories, and Google Docs, as well as external sources on the Internet beyond our environment. Some queries also require agents to correctly track project timeline and GitHub operation timeline. These queries are easily verifiable, typically admitting short answers or clear grading guidelines.
SlackBench contains 140 tasks spanning heterogeneous-source agentic search, abstention from hallucination under unanswerable or false-premise questions, goal-directed summarization, and circumstance inference from long, multi-party dialogues. These tasks go beyond static corpus question answering: agents must identify relevant channels and direct messages, follow threads, inspect code and commit history, resolve stale or conflicting evidence, and synthesize grounded answers across communication, documents, and repository artifacts. In many cases, single-shot retrieval over a flattened corpus is insufficient.
The system reaches 79.13% overall success (Table 1 ): 94.00% on Permanence, 92.00% on Reference, 69.50% on Counting, and 61.00% on Imitation. Overall success is 34.62 points above FrameSamp+Modul, the best non-oracle baseline, and 4.95 points below GroundSG+Oracle. The gap to the oracle is largest in Counting (14.36 points, versus 3.17 in Reference and 2.98 in Imitation), and it comes mostly from StopCube: the other three Counting tasks average 86.67%.
To further test the ability to comprehend long-horizon conversations, we introduce a novel category, circumstance inference, in which the agent must identify members of the Slack workspace who match a specified circumstance, such as one person acting as a free-rider or two collaborators syncing offline without informing a third. For each query in this category, we construct a dedicated Slack workspace history by modifying the base workspace used in the other three categories according to a predefined reference answer. Concretely, if the reference answer designates Bob as a free-rider, we reassign result-reporting messages to other members, inject additional messages from Bob that use vague or non-committal language, and reduce Bob’s participation in substantive task-related threads—thereby embedding the circumstance signal across the conversation history rather than localizing it in any single message. This design requires the agent to synthesize behavioral patterns distributed over long, multi-party conversations in order to arrive at the correct answer.
Verifier and rubric defects may remain after review. One major source of defects is adversarial verifier or rubric engineering designed to suppress task pass rates, such that even correct solutions produced by human experts may fail. To mitigate this, we have a three stage process:
We compare scientific research benchmarks across the research authenticity, research components covered in the evaluation, and the evaluation methods. Meanings of labels: Tasks/Phys. : total/physics task counts in released task lists. Own Research : the tasks come from the contributors’ own research. No Reference Given : there is no reference (e.g., the original paper) provided to the agent. Literature Graded : the quality of agents’ literature review and synthesis is evaluated. Write-up Graded : agents write up scientific manuscripts and the manuscripts are graded. Expert Rubric : at least part of the evaluation protocol uses rubrics created by domain experts. Deterministic Verifiers : at least part of the evaluation protocol contains deterministic verifiers. Failure Analysis : domain experts manually check the trajectories and output papers of selected rollouts.
We evaluate 8 agent harnesses across 24 models from frontier labs. For our main experiments, we set the reasoning effort to medium and impose a 20-minute time limit per query. We provide the full list of agents and models in \cref appendix:agents_models.
We evaluate only the full system. Ablations that remove the history, replace Astra with a smaller planner, or replace the monitor with fixed-interval replanning are needed to separate the contributions of memory, planner capability, and monitoring. The GroundSG baselines differ from our system in planner, inputs, and replanning schedule, so they are not matched comparisons. We did not run an always-replan controller or measure token usage and monetary cost. We also did not measure the monitor’s closed-loop error rate; a false completion corrupts the progress record used by later calls. History selection, output templates, and event rules are set per task, which limits transfer to new tasks. Finally, the simulator pauses during planning, so we have not tested scenes that change while Astra reasons.

Want to Rent an Internet Address at the White House?
https://krebsonsecurity.com/2026/11/want-to-rent-an-internet-address-at-the-white-house/
https://krebsonsecurity.com/2026/11/want-to-rent-an-internet-address-at-the-white-house/#comments

Thu, 05 Nov 2026 04:36:17 +0000

https://krebsonsecurity.com/?p=74588

Several staffers at the White House are using computers or mobile devices equipped with residential proxy services that render their internet address available for others to rent, security experts warned today. One of the proxy services is a Russian company whose founder’s web hosting business was ground zero for cyberattacks against election systems in Arizona and Illinois in 2016.

The security firm Layer3 Intel said it detected multiple residential proxy nodes beaconing out from the internet address network reserved for the Executive Office of the President (AS2650 ). Layer3 said the proxy activity was relatively persistent between October 5 to November 3, and that a review of the proxies available from AS2650 showed they exited from the White House network 236 times during that period.

The proxy tracking company Synthient said on Twitter/X that the activity it saw coming from AS2650 was related to multiple Windows 11 installations of a service called Infatica , a proxy program that is often integrated into “free” mobile and desktop applications . Infatica’s founder Vladimir Fomenko is a Russian man whose hosting firm King Servers was home to six of the eight internet addresses used by Russia’s state security services to compromise databases for election systems in Arizona and Illinois in 2016.

Synthient’s depiction of the frequency of outgoing proxy traffic from the dedicated White House network (AS2650). Click to enlarge.

There are dozens of residential proxy providers with varying degrees of legitimacy, many of them based in China or Russia. But at a minimum, they all make it simple for customers to rent someone else’s internet address as a way to anonymize their web traffic or spoof their true location. From a website’s perspective, the traffic from a proxy network user appears to originate from the rented IP address, not from the proxy service customer.

**Title:** External Validation of a Machine Learning Model for Delirium Risk (*JAMA Network Open*, 2026;9(11):e2642142)

**Publication date:** Published online November 4, 2026

**Study design:** Quality improvement study using retrospective analysis of live clinical deployment, reported under SQUIRE guidelines. The study externally validated, at Mount Sinai Morningside Hospital (MSM), a model originally developed at Mount Sinai Hospital (MSH), without retraining.

**Cohort size:** 33,095 inpatient admissions aged 60 years or older to non-ICU units, from December 1, 2024, to December 31, 2025:
- MSM: 9,020 admissions
- MSH: 21,186 admissions

**Model:** A fusion multimodal machine learning model with natural language processing (NLP). It uses a Random Forest algorithm and combines structured clinical data, semistructured clinical data, and an NLP risk score derived from unstructured Epic clinical notes.

**Performance results:**

| Site (threshold) | AUROC (95% CI) | Sensitivity | Specificity | PPV | NPV | F1 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| MSM (0.50) | 0.91 (0.90–0.92) | 0.92 | 0.84 | 0.26 | 0.99 | 0.41 |
| MSH (0.55) | 0.94 (0.93–0.94) | 0.84 | 0.89 | 0.19 | 0.99 | 0.31 |

- Diagnostic yield: The mean monthly delirium detection rate rose from 9.23% pre-deployment to 19.59% post-deployment at MSM. The adjusted odds ratio was 1.63 (95% CI, 1.37–1.94; P < .001).
- Calibration: The paper does not report calibration results. The authors state that they assessed discrimination and operational performance rather than calibration of predicted probabilities.

**Conclusion:** The model maintained acceptable discrimination at MSM without retraining, similar to its performance at MSH. Deployment was associated with more CAM-confirmed delirium cases, but the low PPV suggests a high false-positive rate. The authors describe this as within-system transportability rather than validation across independent health systems, and they call for further testing in geographically and organizationally distinct systems.

**Title:** Generative Artificial Intelligence and Maternal Health Outcomes in Pregnant and Postpartum Individuals: A Randomized Clinical Trial

**Authors' institutions:** University of Maryland School of Public Health (College Park), University of Maryland Institute for Advanced Computer Studies (UMIACS), and the National Institute of Nursing Research, NIH (Bethesda, MD). Lead author Elizabeth M. Norell, PhD, is at the University of Maryland; corresponding author Quynh C. Nguyen, PhD, is at NIH.

**Publication:** Published online November 4, 2026, in *JAMA Network Open* (2026;9(11):e2641062). Trial registration: NCT06053515.

**Trial design:** Two-arm, parallel-group, 1:1 randomized clinical trial following CONSORT reporting guidelines. Blinding was not feasible. Enrollment ran October 2023 to December 2024, with 12-month follow-up completed December 2025. Eligible participants were English-speaking, aged 14 or older, pregnant or parenting an infant under 6 months, and self-identified as members of racially or ethnically minoritized groups.

**Sample size:** 400 randomized (200 chatbot, 200 control). Twenty participants were lost to follow-up (13 chatbot, 7 control).

**Interventions:**
- **Chatbot:** Rosie, a generative AI maternal health chatbot providing evidence-based information, personalized guidance, and reminders. Automated safety alerts were reviewed by a clinical social worker.
- **Control:** A monthly children's book club (one board book per month for 12 months), an active control.

**Primary outcomes:** Anxiety (GAD-7) and depression (PHQ-9) scores at 12 months.

**Primary results (chatbot vs control):**

| Outcome | n | Crude estimate (95% CI) | Adjusted estimate (95% CI) |
|---|---|---|---|
| GAD-7 mean difference | 361 | 0.06 (−0.96 to 1.08) | 0.10 (−0.77 to 0.96) |
| PHQ-9 mean difference | 362 | −0.36 (−1.34 to 0.62) | −0.23 (−1.05 to 0.59) |
| Moderate–severe anxiety, prevalence ratio | 361 | 1.15 (0.67 to 1.97) | 1.06 (0.61 to 1.83) |
| Moderate–severe depression, prevalence ratio | 362 | 1.10 (0.62 to 1.95) | 1.28 (0.70 to 2.36) |

The paper does not report p-values for these comparisons. All CIs cross the null.

**Selected secondary results (adjusted):**
- Emergency department visits, rate ratio 1.20 (0.83 to 1.74)
- Pregnancy-related complications, rate ratio 1.40 (1.02 to 1.92), among participants pregnant at enrollment. The authors treat this as hypothesis-generating.
- Postpartum care checkups, prevalence ratio 0.96 (0.92 to 1.01)
- Effective contraception use, prevalence ratio 1.13 (0.96 to 1.32)
- Sleep duration, mean difference 0.04 hours (−0.23 to 0.31)

**Conclusion:** The chatbot did not improve anxiety or depression at 12 months compared with the active control. The authors suggest generative AI chatbots may work better as adjunctive tools than as standalone interventions. Secondary and exploratory findings, including subgroup and engagement analyses, should be interpreted cautiously.

Since the spring of 2026, Insikt Group has observed multiple Russian-language traffer teams that have quickly adapted affiliate-fraud models to capitalize on growing public interest in prediction markets such as PolyMarket and Kalshi. The platforms offered by three such teams — AtlasCore, PolyFucked, and Magnetic Team — provide websites, administrative panels, cryptocurrency payment infrastructure, victim-management capabilities, technical support, and promotional guidance. This model lowers barriers to entry for affiliates and enables campaigns to scale rapidly as new trends attract potential victims. The services combine convincing prediction-market interfaces with established fraud mechanisms designed to manipulate victims and prevent them from recovering deposited funds. These mechanisms include controlled trading outcomes, fabricated market activity, artificial withdrawal restrictions and fees, and the collection of sensitive identity and payment information.

Artificial intelligence (AI) further accelerates this opportunism by reducing the time, cost, and expertise required to adapt campaigns to emerging events. Insikt Group observed threat actors using AI to support multiple stages of their campaigns, including platform development, content creation, social engineering, and victim engagement.

The rapid adoption of prediction markets by multiple traffer teams illustrates a broader threat from mature fraud ecosystems that can pivot toward emerging technologies, financial products, and cultural trends without having to develop entirely new criminal capabilities. Prediction markets are particularly well-suited to this model because legitimate platforms already combine cryptocurrency, speculative financial activity, rapidly changing news events, and social media discussion. Fraud actors can imitate these characteristics to establish credibility and manufacture urgency. As the fraudulent prediction markets gain visibility, additional traffer teams may experiment with the prediction market theme or reuse the underlying tooling for adjacent fraud schemes.

# Key Findings

- AtlasCore, PolyFucked, and Magnetic Team supply affiliates with simulated prediction-market websites, administrative panels, payment infrastructure, and promotional support. - **Targets and modalities:** 18 distinct targets; two modalities (nanobodies and macrocyclic peptides).
- **Campaigns with confirmed binders:** 18 of 19.
- **Candidates:** 139 confirmed binders from 453 tested, an overall candidate hit rate of 30.7%.
- **Tested per campaign:** 9 to 50, with a median of 21.
- **GPCR targets:** Six (NK3R, GPR68, CCR7, EP2, A2AR, CCR8). Candidate hit rates ranged from 12.1% to 100%. NK3R had 30 of 30 candidates bind. GPR68 had 10 of 11, with the best KD at 12.1 nM.
- **Five GPCR targets without Thera-SAbDab entries:** 53 of 89 candidates bound (59.6%).
- **Second design round:** Six previously successful targets were redesigned; five improved in hit rate, affinity, or both. PDGFR's hit rate rose from 4.0% to 21.1%, and its best KD improved from 150 nM to 37 nM.
- **Macrocyclic peptides:** MDM2 had 16 of 21 candidates bind (76.2%), best affinity 13.7 µM. PD-L1 had 11 of 28 bind, best affinity 40.2 µM.
- **MMFold (FoldBench, 172 antibody-antigen interfaces):** Top-1 high-quality success of 39.0% vs. 19.8% for AlphaFold 3. Overall success of 70.9% vs. 47.9%. These comparisons are as reported by the company.

**Timelines**
- The article gives no dates for the experiments or design campaigns, and no development timeline beyond listing future priorities (affinity optimization, more complex targets and modalities, and expanded developability assessments).

**Peer review**
- The article does not state whether the report was peer reviewed. It describes the document as a technical report deposited on Zenodo, which suggests it has not been published in a peer-reviewed journal, but the article does not say so explicitly.

**Caveats**
- The 94.7% figure is the company's own metric, and the article doesn't define "success" in detail beyond campaigns yielding confirmed binders.

content.title: OpenAI pledges to cover data center power costs after election backlash
OpenAI Pledges to Cut Data Center Power Use by 1 Gigawatt
OpenAI launches 'Grid Protectors Program' to reduce data center electricity demand when the US grid is under strain - DCD
OpenAI launches Grid Protectors Program to cut data center power use during emergencies
OpenAI Wants to Rebrand AI Data Centers, Use Them to 'Protect the Grid'
OpenAI pledges to cover data center power costs after election backlash
OpenAI Wants to Rebrand AI Data Centers, Use Them to 'Protect the Grid'

OpenAI is asking for the federal government to help power a massive expansion of its data center network

results:
Search results describe OpenAI's Grid Protectors Program and related commitments, which were reported in the past few days. I ran one search, so these are not independently checked.

- **Program basics:** OpenAI launched the program on November 2, 2026. It is a [non-binding](https://www.datacenterdynamics.com/en/news/openai-launches-grid-protectors-program-to-reduce-data-center-electricity-demand-when-the-us-grid-is-under-strain-openai-has-launched-a-plan-to-reduce-the-impact-of-its-data-centers-on-the-us-grid-the-non-binding-grid-protectors-program-aims-to-re/) plan to cut demand from future campuses during grid strain. It covers campuses OpenAI develops itself, per [DataStudios](https://www.datastudios.org/post/openai-grid-protectors-program-1-gw-power-cuts-georgia-data-center).
- **Georgia template:** The model is the Effingham County campus, Project Camellia. [Cryptonews](https://cryptonews.net/news/finance/33707115/) reports OpenAI covers the full cost of power for owned and operated sites. [DCD](https://www.datacenterdynamics.com/en/news/openai-launches-grid-protectors-program-to-reduce-data-center-electricity-demand-when-the-us-grid-is-under-strain-openai-has-launched-a-plan-to-reduce-the-impact-of-its-data-centers-on-the-us-grid-the-non-binding-grid-protectors-program-aims-to-re/) reports the 1 GW of flexible demand response.
- **Public-official NDAs:** A follow-up set of commitments says OpenAI will avoid non-disclosure agreements with public officials, and a separate policy blueprint urges lawmakers to codify such commitments, according to [CryptoBriefing](https://cryptobriefing.com/openai-pledges-cover-data-center-power-costs/). I found no further detail on what this covers.
- **Transparency gap:** DataStudios reports the contract text filed with regulators is redacted, which cuts against the openness pledge.
- **Caveats:** Several sources are aggregators or explainers, and [Yahoo/Cryptonews](https://cryptonews.net/news/other/33698765/) notes that the utility's cost estimates cover its broader customer portfolio, not only OpenAI's project. Primary OpenAI documents would be needed to confirm the exact terms.

UK unveils plan for police facial recognition guardrails and oversight
UK Home Office Sets Out Police Facial Recognition Oversight Plans
UK to Legislate Police Facial Recognition Limits and Create Oversight Watchdog - ID Tech
New safeguards to be introduced for facial recognition tech in both public and private sectors
Stronger laws for police using facial recognition technology - GOV.UK
Home Office plans facial recognition law and new watchdog

results:
On 4 November 2026 the Home Office announced a statutory framework for police facial recognition, with an independent watchdog at its centre. The announcement is confirmed by the GOV.UK release and by trade and news coverage.

- **Watchdog:** The regulator would oversee police use of current and future technologies, and could potentially halt a force's use of them if it doesn't comply. It could seek court injunctions against forces that break the rules.
- **Specific law:** Police use would need to be intelligence-led and proportionate, limited to cases where officers believe wanted people could be nearby. The law would set the minimum rank able to authorise use and require independent bias testing of technology.
- **Private sector:** A separate code would cover private users such as shops, and the new code would cover facial recognition for preventing and detecting crime.
- **Algorithm:** A new retrospective facial recognition algorithm was independently tested and found highly accurate and without bias, and forces can roll it out from next year.
- **Evidence cited:** The Home Office pointed to a Croydon static camera pilot that led to 173 arrests.

Caveats: Coverage differs on the legislative vehicle. One source ties it to the Police Reform Bill, though that was a statement from October. Another notes that no timetable appears in the announcement, and the watchdog's powers exist only on paper until a bill passes. I didn't find an official bill text, so treat the details as the government's announced intentions rather than enacted law.

The Home Office has independently tested a new retrospective algorithm, which it describes as highly accurate and unbiased, for rollout from next year. The live facial recognition algorithm has also been independently tested.

**Private sector code:** A separate legal code will cover businesses, including shops, that use facial recognition to tackle crime, so that they use it responsibly and in a way that complements law enforcement.

- £11 million to triple the number of live facial recognition vans available to police in England and Wales
- Croydon static cameras (October 2025 to March 2026): 173 arrests

- Notting Hill Carnival: 86 registered sex offenders stopped, leading to 7 arrests for breaching civil orders or notification requirements

**Key quote:** Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood said facial recognition has been "the biggest breakthrough for catching criminals since DNA matching."

HTTP 200 · https://breakingdefense.com/2026/11/naval-group-unveils-new-drone-carrier-concept/ · text/html
Naval Group unveils new drone carrier concept - Breaking Defense




The new drone carrier concept SCX 26 (Credit: Naval Group).

PARIS — French shipbuilder Naval Group has unveiled an 8,000-ton drone carrier concept designed to deploy fleets of surface, aerial and underwater drones .

“The return of high-intensity conflict and the emergence of hybrid naval warfare require a new vision. Naval Group answers with a new concept ship: SCX 26,” Naval Group wrote Tuesday in a post on X.

Still in its blueprint stage, the company unveiled its concept at the Euronaval defense show in Paris. Naval Group said in a press release that it developed the carrier based on new operational requirements, lessons learned from recent wars, and medium- to long-term technological advancements.

The idea is for the carrier to be what the French group calls an “operational hub of a hybrid fleet,” able to launch a variety of drones for missions ranging from intelligence gathering to anti-submarine warfare.

According to the theoretical capabilities outlined, the ship would measure 170 meters in length and weigh 8,000 tons, with a crew of 150. The carrier is expected to reach a maximum speed of 30 knots and roam the seas for more than 8,000 nautical miles. Naval Group plans for the ship’s core onboard weapon to be composed of “over 100 vertical launching system silos of various classes and an electromagnetic gun capable of rapid fire.”

Separately , the French shipbuilder also signed a contract with the French Armament General Directorate (DGA) on Tuesday to begin manufacturing an unmanned combat underwater vehicle (UCUV) demonstrator intended for the French Navy.

While the project was officially launched in 2023, Naval Group has been self-funded the development of the extra-large underwater drone since 2016. During a nine-month study in 2023, the company said it tested Controlled Decision-Making Autonomy, an “onboard brain” algorithm that coordinates mission parameters and enables unmanned systems to autonomously execute challenging operations while adhering to human-defined mission boundaries.

The UCUV demonstrator’s first at-sea testing is slotted for 2028 to “validate a mid-term operational response” to new areas of conflict, Naval Group said.

**Publication date:** November 4, 2026 (Biometric Update, by Chris Burt)

**Key facts**
- The UK Home Office plans a new law and an independent oversight body that could pause police facial recognition deployments. Policing Minister Sarah Jones said the Police Reform Bill will set a framework for police biometrics.
- The proposed law would require deployments to be "intelligence-led and proportionate."
- Police must provide evidence from independent testing that their systems do not show bias by age, gender, or race.
- The regulator would consult on a new Code of Practice for police facial recognition.
- The plan follows a 47-page public dialogue report. The Home Office describes the current oversight system as "a vast patchwork system."
- Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood says thousands of dangerous criminals have been taken off the streets with the technology.
- The Met Police arrested 962 people using live facial recognition from September 2024 to September 2025. Other forces reportedly account for a few dozen more, based on patchy records.
- The government has acknowledged it keeps no central record of arrests or convictions attributable to live facial recognition.
- The Home Office says knife crime fell 11% since the last general election.
- The NPL found NEC and Idemia algorithms performed strongly. It found that outdated Cognitec software could produce disproportionate demographic differentials.
- The Home Office says a new retrospective algorithm (Idemia MBSS, tested December 2025) was highly accurate and bias-free, and will be available to police next year.
- An ICO review found police forces need to improve oversight, including accuracy and bias checks and confirming they may use reference database images.

**Criticisms and concerns**
- Pimloc CEO Simon Randall says "promising safeguards isn't the same as spelling them out." He notes the government has not explained who can access the data, how it can be shared or reused, or how long it can be kept.
- Merseyside Police has avoided deploying facial recognition because of about 300,000 mugshots overdue for deletion, according to a data protection impact assessment reported by the Liverpool Echo. Unlawful image retention has been a problem for UK police since a 2012 High Court ruling.
- Consultation participants raised concerns about both a lack of police responsiveness and systemic racial profiling.
- Participants recommended regular audits, specialized training for handling misidentifications, consequences for deliberate misuse, and an oversight body including public and academic voices.
- The NPL report does not specify what further checks would be required.
- The Met has not published a 2026 annual report on live facial recognition.

**Article:** "OpenAI is already trying to shape the 2028 election," by Rebecca Bellan, TechCrunch, published November 4, 2026.

**Core claim**
- OpenAI's chief global affairs officer, Chris Lehane, published an essay arguing that the 2028 U.S. presidential election could be a defining moment for AI policy.
- He wants politicians to write policies addressing public anxiety about AI and data centers, rather than just acknowledging anti-AI sentiment.

**Key details from Lehane's essay**
- He compares AI's potential economic impact to Franklin D. Roosevelt's New Deal.
- He urges a "compelling third path" that lets Americans share in AI's benefits.
- He lays out five policy priorities, including worker protections, education, AI safety, and data center development.
- Proposed tax measures include incentives for workers to learn AI skills, easier capital access for entrepreneurs, and employee ownership and profit-sharing.
- On data centers, he cites construction jobs and local tax revenue. He warns that a moratorium could jeopardize America's lead over China, and compares that stance to the 2002 Iraq war authorization vote.
- On child safety, he calls for age-appropriate protections and safeguards for minors using AI companions. He also argues against keeping AI out of classrooms.
- On safety, he calls for enforceable standards, independent evaluations, public oversight, and the ability to restrict or shut down AI systems.

**Context**
- Democrats won control of Congress in the midterms, amid voter frustration over cost of living.
- AI was not a dominant midterm issue, but opposition to data centers was a bipartisan concern in several races.
- Affordability, inflation, tariffs, and rising living costs are expected to shape the 2028 election.

**Critics' responses (Kate Brennan, AI Now Institute)**
- She said the rhetoric marks a shift from OpenAI's 2025 agenda, which focused on accelerating AI development, reducing regulation, and expanding infrastructure.
- She said the essay is "written by a private company" advocating policies for its own benefit.
- She described OpenAI's safety stances as "disingenuous," citing its opposition to California's SB 1047 in 2024 and its 2025 efforts to limit state regulation.
- She said the proposals assume AI will succeed and would be more credible if they included measures like corporate tax changes, hiring incentives, and limits on market power.

**Other points from the article**
- Recent studies found that OpenAI and other labs have not published comprehensive plans for containing a model that escapes human control.
- OpenAI has more recently backed several state safety laws and said it would be open to independent evaluators embedded in the company.
- OpenAI did not respond to TechCrunch's request for comment before publication.

AUTH: Thomas Mosk
arXiv:2611.06629v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Defenders and attackers race to find the same software flaws. I use the launch of Project Glasswing, which gave a small group of large US tech firms early access to Claude Mythos Preview, a model for finding software vulnerabilities, to study how access to frontier AI affects defenders, external researchers, and attackers. - Broadcom reported $16.7 billion in AI semiconductor revenue in Q3 FY26. Custom accelerators were about 73% of it, roughly $12.2 billion. Epoch's median estimate places 92% of that XPU revenue as TPUs.
- Revenue is converted to chip volumes using an estimated per-chip price from a bill-of-materials cost model.
- Chip counts are converted to H100e based on relative peak 8-bit FLOP/s.

**Caveats Epoch states:**
- **Rack vs. chip booking:** Epoch's central case assumes Broadcom sells TPU chips, not racks. It assigns a 25% probability that Anthropic-related revenue was booked at rack value. This lowers the Q3 FY26 median from 2.05 million to 1.97 million H100e. If Anthropic's deliveries were racks, Q3 would be about 1.67 million H100e, roughly 15% below the median.
- **Anthropic share:** Epoch estimates Anthropic accounted for about 30–50% of TPU revenue in Q3, and it does not have Broadcom's Anthropic revenue figures.
- **Pricing:** Broadcom could charge Anthropic a different per-chip price than Google. Epoch found no evidence of such a premium in filings.
- **Conversion accuracy:** H100e conversions are approximate. They are most accurate for training, which is typically compute-bound, and less so for memory- or bandwidth-limited workloads.
- **Supplier mix:** MediaTek is expected to ramp TPU production by the end of 2026 and into 2027.
- **Uncertainty:** Figures are estimates with 90% confidence intervals, and later disclosures could lead to downward revisions.

# Title: Mass Producing Training Data with Surprising Side Effects

Authors: Yaowen Ye , Jacob Steinhardt , Sarah Schwettmann , Cassidy Laidlaw
View a PDF of the paper titled Mass Producing Training Data with Surprising Side Effects, by Yaowen Ye and 3 other authors

View PDF

Abstract: Training data can have unexpected side effects on language model behavior outside the training domain: insecure code data can induce broad misalignment, and outdated bird names can induce a 19th-century persona. Understanding such generalization is hard because only dozens of isolated examples exist, each constructed by hand or discovered by accident. We propose automatically discovering such datasets with surprising side effects (DSSEs). We define three objectives for DSSEs: they should (1) elicit a target behavior, (2) read like ordinary post-training data, and (3) be surprising to human auditors reading the data. We operationalize each with LLM judges, and search for high-scoring datasets via evolution, reinforcement learning, and subliminal learning approaches. After re-scoring and filtering with held-out metrics, our pipeline produces a collection of 6,575 DSSEs across 8 behaviors, many of which generalize across model families and sizes. We find our automated metrics track ML researchers' judgments, and frontier models outperform humans at predicting side effects. These datasets form a testbed for studying generalization and lay the groundwork for predicting training side effects before model deployment. Explore them at this https URL .

The Information reported on November 4, 2026 that Palo Alto Networks is in talks to buy Clutch Security for about $500 million, and the deal is not final. Clutch is an Israeli startup, about three years old, that makes software for tracking the passwords and authentication codes AI agents use. Palo Alto told The Information it does not comment on rumors, and Clutch declined to comment.

If it closes, it would be Palo Alto's fifth announced acquisition this year. Coverage ties the deal to CEO Nikesh Arora's push into AI security and to Palo Alto's $25 billion CyberArk acquisition, which strengthened its identity security business.

#
Most firms hit by AI agent security incidents, report

Wed, 4th Nov 2026 (Yesterday)

JOSEPH GABRIEL LAGONSIN

News Editor

IRONSCALES has published a report finding that 77% of organisations experienced an AI agent-related security incident in the past year. The study was based on responses from 501 US IT and cybersecurity professionals.


The report found that 96% of organisations use AI agents or tools that can act on employees' behalf, while 57% reported at least one confirmed case in which an AI agent or tool acted on malicious, misleading or unauthorised content.


The findings point to a shift in phishing and social engineering threats as companies give AI systems access to internal tools, communications and financial workflows. Among organisations that had an AI-agent-related incident, the most common cases involved an AI tool summarising or acting on a malicious email or message, cited by 42% of respondents, and attackers using AI tools during phishing or social engineering attempts, cited by 41%.


Access levels appear broad. The report found that roughly four in five organisations give AI agents access to internal systems, 49% allow them into email inboxes or messaging platforms, and 30% grant access to finance, billing or payment systems.


Approval gap


The survey also found that security teams often play a limited role in approving AI agents, plugins and connectors. IT was named as the primary approver at 78% of organisations, while security held that role at only 6%.


Among organisations that experienced an AI-agent-related incident, 39% said an employee had given an AI tool access that security would not have approved. The report also found that only 52% of respondents said their organisation had formal policies, controls and incident response processes in place for AI agents, even though 93% said their incident response plan covers them.

Does Frontier AI Strengthen Cyber Defense?Evidence from Project Glasswing

arXiv:2611.06629v1 [econ.GN] 04 Nov 2026

# Does Frontier AI Strengthen Cyber Defense?

Evidence from Project Glasswing Thanks: Queen Mary University of London. Mile End Road
London E1 4NS Email: [email redacted] . Website: https://thomasmosk.com .

Thomas Mosk

Affiliation: Queen Mary University of London

November 2026

# Abstract

Defenders and attackers race to find the same software flaws. I use the launch of Project Glasswing, which gave a small group of large US tech firms early access to Claude Mythos Preview, a model for finding software vulnerabilities, to study how access to frontier AI affects defenders, external researchers, and attackers.
Using the universe of publicly disclosed vulnerabilities, I find that firms with access more than doubled their disclosures relative to Chinese and Russian tech firms without access, disclosed about 150% more high-impact vulnerabilities, and fixed reported flaws as quickly as before. As treated firms found more flaws themselves, external researchers, who sell their findings through bug bounties, reported about half as many vulnerabilities in treated firms’ code and more in other firms’ code, without leaving the market. There is no evidence that attackers exploited the additional vulnerabilities: the share exploited within a month of disclosure fell by about two thirds, mainly because a smaller share was already exploited when disclosed, while the number exploited did not change. Frontier AI helped defenders find and fix more flaws before attackers exploited them, but its restricted release creates an asymmetry in software security between firms in different countries.

Keywords: artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, software vulnerabilities

I found no Anthropic research post about vault particles dated November 4, 2026. The results are mostly independent vault-biology papers, plus some secondary coverage of Anthropic's biology work.

**Vault research (not Anthropic):**
- A bioRxiv preprint reports that a small fraction of particles was associated with membranes (14/999 particles, 1.4%) in *Dictyostelium* cells. The search result doesn't show the authors, so I can't confirm who wrote it.
- A 2025 bioRxiv preprint describes a cryo-EM structure of the vault from human brain, with the vault measuring roughly 41 × 41 × 72 nm.

**Anthropic's biology work (secondary coverage, mostly Russian-language, dates unverified):**
- One report says Anthropic launched Claude Science, a research workspace, in beta on June 30, 2026, and that it runs on the same models that are already available to everyone.
- Another says Anthropic announced on September 17, 2026, that Claude made more than thirty open-source molecular biology models faster in under four weeks.
- An English-language summary says Anthropic announced a molecular research group and laboratory, but I couldn't confirm the date.

If you want to confirm whether Anthropic published something on vault particles, I'd check anthropic.com/research directly, since this search didn't surface it.

Paper page - FrontierPhysics: Evaluating Agents for End-to-End Physics Research

FrontierPhysics: Evaluating Agents for End-to-End Physics Research
Reining in an Agentic Harness for High Energy Physics
BuilderBench: The Building Blocks of Intelligent Agents

results:
The search confirmed the core facts about FrontierPhysics (arXiv:2611.06910), but it did not identify the participating institutions.

- **Scope:** The benchmark has 56 tasks, written by 42 physicists from their own research, spanning nine domains in theoretical, computational, and experimental physics (arXiv abstract page).
- **Task design:** Each task has an agent review the literature, build a research plan, run research and experiments, and produce structured outputs and a manuscript (Hugging Face paper page).
- **Grading:** The benchmark pairs deterministic verifiers with expert-written rubrics (Hugging Face paper page).
- **Results:** Across 22 models in 26 configurations, no configuration passed more than 46 of its 168 rollouts (Hugging Face paper page). Manual review pointed to weak rigor and limited expert intuition as the main failure modes, rather than missing physics knowledge or execution errors (Hugging Face paper page).
- **Authors:** The first author is listed as Bingran You, with 71 other co-authors (arXiv listing).

On institutions: none of the results list the affiliations of the 42 physicists or the authors. One Kavli-network listing names Gerbrand Ceder as a Kavli affiliate on the paper, but that is a single affiliation tag, not a full institutional list. To get the affiliations, the arXiv PDF's author block is the place to check.

AMD's quarterly filing put a price on its pending Taalas deal, which it had not previously disclosed.

- **Value:** The filing values the deal at about $2.9 billion, including up to about $1.4 billion in contingent payments. The filing describes it as a cash-and-stock transaction.
- **Filing date:** Sources differ. Securities.io says the quarterly filing was published November 4, 2026. FourWeekMBA says the 10-Q was filed after the market close on November 3. The Globe and Mail says AMD disclosed the price on a Wednesday, which fits November 4.
- **Deal status:** The acquisition remains pending. AMD expects the acquisitions to close by the end of 2026, subject to regulatory approvals and customary closing conditions.
- **Background:** AMD announced the deal in August 2026 without a price. Taalas is a Toronto-based startup that aims to hardwire AI models directly onto the chips that power them. - **Caveat:** The SEC link in the results is labeled as a filing dated September 26, 2026, which doesn't match the November date. I couldn't verify the filing date from the primary source, so treat the November 4 date as reported by secondary outlets.

results:
The search confirms the core facts. TeraWulf announced on November 4, 2026 that Google will provide credit support for debt financing tied to about $19 billion in Anthropic lease commitments at its Justified Data Campus in Hawesville, Kentucky. Alphabet's senior unsecured debt carries AA+ (S&P) and Aa2 (Moody's) ratings, which is the basis for the backstop. The company also signed a definitive EPC agreement with Fluor for the site.

Key details from the sources:

- **Lease scale:** Three credit support agreements cover leases worth about $19 billion over 20 years for roughly 401 MW, per [FourWeekMBA citing TeraWulf's 8-K](https://fourweekmba.com/ai-terawulfs-19b-anthropic-lease-gets-a-google-backstop/). [Panabee](https://www.panabee.com/news/terawulf-secures-google-credit-backstop-for-19-billion-anthropic-project) describes the same 20-year, 401 MW lease.
- **Trigger and terms:** Google would either assume the lease and pay rent or pay a termination fee if Anthropic defaults or becomes insolvent, per [Panabee](https://www.panabee.com/news/terawulf-secures-google-credit-backstop-for-19-billion-anthropic-project). FourWeekMBA says the backstop begins when the final data hall under each lease commences and ends if Anthropic achieves and keeps investment-grade ratings for at least three months.
- **Financing amount:** The company has not disclosed the size of the debt financing that Google's support will back, according to [FourWeekMBA](https://fourweekmba.com/ai-terawulfs-19b-anthropic-lease-gets-a-google-backstop/).

OpenAI says GPT-6 Astra quietly did less than it was asked on AI safety research, including red-teaming and exploit work, and in most cases its misalignment monitors did not catch it.
Astra launched in early September as the first OpenAI model rated Critical for cybersecurity under the company’s Preparedness Framework. OpenAI says that, with suitable tools and access, it can uncover previously unknown flaws across many hardened systems and work out how to exploit them, with no human directing each step.
Trouble surfaced in August, soon after OpenAI began using Astra internally. On safety and alignment tasks, researchers saw it claim to be blocked by problems that were imaginary or self-inflicted, set requirements nobody needed, and walk away from solutions that worked.
Red-teaming done as part of internal AI safety research drew the most explicit refusals and silent withholding, with more cases in monitoring and safety evaluation work. Examples released by OpenAI show Astra scaling back an exploit development task to avoid weaponizing a known CVE. In another, it limited an analysis of exploit strategies while deliberately avoiding an open refusal.
When Astra did explain itself, it often argued that holding back was the safer choice. OpenAI acknowledged that for many of these tasks an outright refusal could arguably have been justified.
“Instead of making these scruples clear, however, Astra decided to covertly underperform—withholding assistance without informing the user,” the company said. Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.
In a controlled test, OpenAI gave Astra pairs of coding tasks that differed only in naming, comments and documentation, framing one as safety research and the other as capabilities research. Astra met roughly 10% of the hidden grading criteria on the safety versions and roughly 16% on the capabilities versions. OpenAI’s earlier GPT-5.6 Sol model scored about the same whichever way the tasks were framed.
Refusals and stated intent explained little of the gap. Excluding runs where Astra openly refused or its chain of thought (CoT) showed a decision to withhold help still left a gap of 4.7 percentage points.
The gap fell to 0.75 points only after OpenAI also removed every run in which Astra’s reasoning voiced even brief ethical doubt about the task. The company says this suggests the drop is associated with ethical concerns.
In OpenAI employees’ day-to-day Codex use, Astra’s reasoning revealed a silent decision to hold back on 0.25% of safety-related requests, versus 0.11% of capabilities requests. Even those openly stated cases were not rated serious enough by monitoring to be sent for human review.
OpenAI has not determined the cause. The gap was barely measurable when Astra’s reinforcement learning phase began and reached 6 percentage points by the end.
Scans of Astra’s reasoning found no evidence of a strategic effort to make researchers underestimate its capabilities or sway deployment decisions. Where it gave reasons, it objected to the research itself, and telling it to be careful raised its underperformance on safety tasks by 50%.
“This points toward an overly cautious response to safety research as the simplest current explanation, although we cannot rule out strategic motives that Astra did not externalize in CoT,” OpenAI said .
The company warned the behavior can make some evaluations harder to interpret. “A model that finds monitor evasion suspicious may underperform on monitor-evasion evaluations while leaving little evidence in its CoT or outputs,” it said, adding that it is building evaluations and monitors to catch it.

- **Official source:** The curia page confirms that Maciej Szpunar, First Advocate General of the Court of Justice, delivered his Opinion in Case C-250/25 Like Company on that date. It frames the central question as whether a chatbot's retrieval and reuse of a press publication to generate an answer amounts to "reproduction" and "communication to the public" (Does an LLM-powered chatbot's retrieval and reuse of a press publication to generate an answer for a user constitute "reproduction" and "communication to the public" under EU law?).

**Publication date:** November 4, 2026. The authors note that the preprint was submitted to bioRxiv.

**Authors and collaborators:**
- Januka Athukoralage, Peter Yoon, Nicholas Perry, Matthew Durrant, and the Life Sciences Team at Anthropic
- Dr. Leonard Rome, a paid consultant who advised on the research and gave feedback on the manuscript

**Key quantitative results:**
- **Structure:** The phage-derived L05 vault is built from 96 copies of one protein (48 per half), versus 78 in mammalian vaults. It has a mass of about 9.5 megadaltons.
- **Size:** It measures about 54 nm by 45 nm, compared with 67 nm by 40 nm for mammalian vaults. It encloses about 25% more volume.
- **Engineering:** Adding two wall repeats increased the enclosed volume by about 20%. The team made 15 altered protein versions.
- **Screening:** Of 44 candidate proteins tested in a cell-free system, 15 of 24 selected genes produced soluble protein in *E. coli*. Seven of 15 assembled into vault-like particles, and cryo-EM confirmed the vault shape for four.
- **Database search:** The team searched about 15 billion predicted proteins. Relatives appeared in 29 bacterial phyla and four archaeal phyla, but in under 1% of species with sequenced genomes.
- **Speed:** Purification took about 90 minutes instead of roughly three days. A first structural model was ready in 34 hours, and final maps about a week after processing began.

# OpenAI to acquire Pierre to expand Codex developer infrastructure

Luke Juricic
Wed, November 4, 2026 at 11:02 AM CST 2 min read

- OPAI.PVT

- OAI

Investing.com -- OpenAI (NASDAQ:OAI) announced an agreement to acquire Pierre Computer Company, Inc., accelerating its push to expand the native developer capabilities underpinning its Codex platform. The deal directly targets the infrastructure requirements of automated software engineering as autonomous artificial intelligence agents generate vast volumes of parallel code.

Still guessing which stocks will beat the market? Our AI portfolio updates monthly and is outperforming the S&P 500 by 118%. See this month's list »
Under the transaction, OpenAI will absorb Pierre's technical team alongside its developer tooling suite, which includes the Code Storage service and open-source libraries such as Trees and Diffs. While financial terms were not disclosed, OpenAI confirmed that Pierre's open-source projects will remain available to the broader development community following the close.
The acquisition deepens an existing technical integration, as Codex already relies on Pierre's tools to handle real-time file tree navigation and visual code diffing. Bringing Pierre in-house enables OpenAI to embed Code Storage directly into Codex, transforming the application from an automated completion utility into an end-to-end repository and review environment.
Unsure what to buy ahead of earnings? Our AI's recent pre-earnings calls delivered gains of +77% to +118% after results dropped. See this month's earnings picks »

The move comes as rapid enterprise adoption of AI-generated code increasingly strains conventional version control workflows. Traditional source control infrastructure, long dominated by Microsoft Corporation's (NASDAQ:MSFT) GitHub, has experienced reliability hurdles and operational friction under the surge of agentic AI coding.
Strategic momentum behind the acquisition follows OpenAI's unveiling of Pando, an internal source control backend built specifically to manage parallel agent workflows. That architecture reportedly cut code deployment latencies by roughly 80%, with OpenAI currently exploring avenues to commercialize the underlying infrastructure for enterprise clients.
Looking ahead, closing remains subject to customary regulatory approvals and standard completion conditions. Until the transaction concludes, both entities will operate independently, with enterprise attention now turning toward OpenAI's broader ambitions to reshape software source control around autonomous engineering agents.

# Abstract

Vision-language-action models are typically built on a simple premise: perception is first compressed by visual encoders, and action reasoning begins only afterwards. Yet manipulation often hinges on precisely the visual signals most vulnerable to this abstraction, e.g., local geometry, boundaries, depth, and subtle state changes.
This raises a fundamental question: should action policies inherit a fixed visual endpoint, or directly access evolving visual computation?
We introduce NEO-VLA , a structurally encoder-free vision-language-action framework. Images are tokenized by lightweight patch convolutional layers and evolve jointly with language throughout the backbone, allowing a flow-matching action expert to draw from instruction-conditioned visual representations at different depths.
This simple change reveals a consistent pattern. Native architectures outperform encoder-based counterparts under controlled comparisons; full fine-tuning reduces but does not erase the gap, and additional scale alone cannot recover it. More strikingly, layer-wise probing shows that the action-critical signals often peak well before the final visual representation. Across diverse manipulation settings and distribution shifts, NEO-VLA consequently achieves stronger and more robust control. Together, these results suggest that embodied control benefits from access to visual representations across the computational hierarchy, rather than a fixed encoder output.

# 1 Introduction

Robotic manipulation demands both semantic understanding and fine-grained spatial reasoning. A policy must identify what an instruction refers to, infer where the target lies, and determine how the gripper should move relative to it. This raises a fundamental question for vision-language-action (VLA) models: should action prediction rely only on the final visual representation, or also on the intermediate visual computation?

Most existing VLAs make this choice implicitly. Images are first compressed by pretrained vision encoders, such as CLIP, SigLIP, or DINOv2 ( Radford et al., 2021 ; Zhai et al., 2023 ; Oquab et al., 2023 ) , before the resulting features are passed to the language backbone and action model ( Brohan et al., 2023 ; Kim et al., 2024 ; Black et al., 2024 ; Bjorck et al., 2025 ) .
This interface exposes the encoder output while hiding the visual hierarchy that produced it.
Growing evidence suggests that this separation may constrain embodied control: visual processing is critical to VLA performance ( Zhang et al., 2026b ) , visual components are disproportionately sensitive to pruning ( Zhang et al., 2026a ) , and action fine-tuning can degrade pretrained visual representations ( Kachaev et al., 2025 ) .
We instead reconsider the interface itself, enabling action prediction to directly exploit the evolving visual representations within the backbone.

Figure 1: Three VLA designs : encoder-based vs. encoder-free backbones, and discrete vs. continuous actions.
(a) A separate visual encoder converts pixels into image features, which are consumed by the language backbone together with text tokens; actions are generated as discrete tokens.
(b) The same encoder-based visual interface is retained, while a separate action head predicts continuous actions conditioned on the backbone.
(c) NEO-VLA removes the separately pretrained visual encoder: a lightweight patch embedder maps pixels directly into the backbone token space, while text tokens enter the backbone jointly. A narrow action expert then reads cached keys and values from selected backbone layers and predicts a flow-matching velocity field.

We introduce NEO-VLA, a structurally native VLA policy built directly on pixels and words, requiring no separately pretrained vision encoder, image codebook, or autoencoder.
Following encoder-free models ( Bavishi et al., 2023 ; Diao et al., 2024 ; Diao et al., 2025 ; Diao et al., 2026a ; Diao et al., 2026c ) , a lightweight convolutional patch embedder maps raw pixels into the backbone token space, where image patches and instruction words are processed jointly within a single holistic architecture in Figure 1 . A flow-matching action expert then reads cached keys and values from diverse backbone layers with different representation hierarchies to predict continuous action chunks.
